title: Can you hear the shape of a drum?
text:
← 8 Drum · The Shape of a Sound · Spectrum of an operator · Map · 10 Scales →
Listen first: play each drum with every mode equally loud. Then click a drum to strike it at a point, and compare.

title: Can you hear the shape of a drum?
section: 1 · Newton’s law: the equation of motion
text:
1 · Newton’s law: the equation of motion
Mathematics used: the Laplacian (page 8), and counting.
This page asks what the spectrum says about the drum. First, the equation, which page 8 derived step by step.
Let the drumhead be a region \Omega of the plane, in one piece, and let u(x, y, t) be the height of the head above the point (x, y) at time t. On page 8, Newton’s law for one small patch of the head, pulled by the tension in its edges, gave the drum’s equation 
u_{tt} = c^2\,\Delta u \ \text{ inside } \Omega, \qquad u = 0 \ \text{ on the rim},
 where \Delta u = u_{xx} + u_{yy} is the Laplacian, and c^2 is the tension divided by the mass per unit area. The Laplacian is positive where u at a point sits below the average of u around it, and negative where it sits above; the bigger the gap, the bigger the Laplacian. So the equation says: each point of the head accelerates toward the average height around it.
What we assumed is listed on page 8: small slopes, a tension that is the same everywhere and does not change as the head moves, no bending stiffness, no air, and no damping.

title: Can you hear the shape of a drum?
text:
2 · The operator
In the series’ form u_{tt} = -A\,u, the operator is A = -c^2\Delta, acting on shapes that are zero on the rim. The rim condition is part of the operator: the same rule on a different shape is a different operator.

The drum’s operator: A = -c^2\Delta on the drumhead \Omega, acting on shapes with u = 0 on the rim.
In words: the force per unit mass pulling each point of the head back toward rest is c^2 times how far that point sits from the average around it.

title: Can you hear the shape of a drum?
text:
3 · Its spectrum
When is there a mode? A mode is a shape X that the operator only rescales, A X = \lambda X, with \lambda the eigenvalue. Write \lambda = c^2 k^2, so that the shape must satisfy 
-\Delta X = k^2 X \ \text{ inside } \Omega, \qquad X = 0 \ \text{ on the rim}.
 The numbers k^2 for which this has a solution other than X = 0 are the eigenvalues of -\Delta on \Omega, and the solutions X are its eigenfunctions, the mode shapes. They depend only on the shape \Omega; the factor c^2 only scales them.
List them. Put the eigenvalues in order, k_1^2 \le k_2^2 \le k_3^2 \le \cdots, each repeated as many times as it occurs (its multiplicity). The mode with k_n^2 has the operator’s eigenvalue \lambda_n = c^2k_n^2 and swings at 
f_n = \frac{\sqrt{\lambda_n}}{2\pi} = \frac{c\,k_n}{2\pi}.


The drum’s spectrum: the eigenvalues \lambda_n = c^2k_n^2 of A, where -\Delta X_n = k_n^2 X_n inside \Omega and X_n = 0 on the rim, listed \lambda_1 \le \lambda_2 \le \cdots with repeats. The frequencies are f_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}/2\pi = c\,k_n/2\pi.
In words: apart from the one overall factor c, the frequencies are decided by the shape of \Omega alone.

Kac’s question, precisely. Suppose we know c, so that hearing every frequency means knowing every k_n^2. Does the list k_1^2, k_2^2, k_3^2, \dots determine \Omega? It can only do so up to sliding, turning or flipping the drum, which changes no frequency. (Kac wrote that he had first heard the question posed this way about ten years earlier, from Salomon Bochner.)

title: Can you hear the shape of a drum?
text:
4 · On the spectrum diagram
Here are both drums’ first twelve frequencies, as multiples of the lowest, \sqrt{\lambda_n/\lambda_1} = k_n/k_1: 1×, 1.20×, 1.43×, 1.60×, 1.69×, 1.90×, 2.04×, …. Like the drum on page 8, they sit off the gray whole-number lines, so neither drum has a clear pitch. And the two lists are the same to every digit computed: the stems under drum A and drum B stand in the same places. In the demo, each stem’s height is how strongly a strike at the clicked point starts that mode (below, every mode is drawn equally tall): all equal until you click, then different on the two drums, because it depends on the mode’s shape at the struck point.


  
  Both drums' first twelve frequencies, as multiples of the lowest, every mode drawn equally tall: drum A and drum B have exactly these stems (Driscoll's values).

title: Can you hear the shape of a drum?
text:
5 · What we hear
Same frequencies, not the same sound. A struck drum moves as a sum of its modes, 
u = \sum_n a_n X_n \cos(2\pi f_n t + \phi_n),
 so its sound is a sum of tones at the frequencies f_n, each fading at its own rate, with a strength a_n that depends on where it is struck; what you hear also depends on where you listen. The demo’s sound is made exactly this way, from the frequencies in stage 3. The two drums share the frequencies f_n. The mode shapes X_n differ, so the strengths from a strike at a given point differ, and so does the timbre, the color of the sound. Played with every mode equally loud, every a_n = 1, the two drums sound identical. What the drums share is the answer to “which frequencies can this drum make”, which is exactly what the spectrum records.

title: Can you hear the shape of a drum?
text:
What the spectrum knows
Counting the frequencies: area and rim. Count the eigenvalues of -\Delta up to a limit \Lambda: 
N(\Lambda) = \#\{n : k_n^2 \le \Lambda\},
 where \# means “the number of”. (A frequency limit f corresponds to \Lambda = (2\pi f/c)^2, since f_n = c\,k_n/2\pi.) For a high limit, 
N(\Lambda) \approx \frac{|\Omega|}{4\pi}\,\Lambda \;-\; \frac{P}{4\pi}\sqrt{\Lambda},
 where |\Omega| is the drum’s area and P the length of its rim. In words: the number of modes below a high limit grows in proportion to the area, so twice the area gives about twice as many modes; and it falls short of the area’s share by an amount in proportion to the rim’s length, because holding the rim still costs the drum some modes.
The first term is Weyl’s law. Hermann Weyl proved it in 1911, and later work extended it to every drum. So the area can be heard: it is 4\pi times the rate at which N(\Lambda) grows. The second term is subtler. For the count itself it is proved only for some drums: Victor Ivrii proved it in 1980 for smooth rims on which closed billiard paths are rare (fold below). For a slightly smoothed version of the count it is proved for every drum whose rim is smooth or made of straight pieces, and that is enough to hear the rim’s length. Where the second term holds, “\approx” means that the error, divided by \sqrt\Lambda, shrinks to zero as \Lambda grows.
The demo counts the modes of three drums with the same area. Once the area’s share, the same for all three, is taken away, the drum with the longest rim sits lowest.


  
  
    Modes below the limit
    Minus the area's share
  
  Frequency limit
  
  Three drums of equal area: a disk, a square, a long rectangle. Steps: the true counts. Dashed: Weyl's formula, area and rim together. Gray: the area's share alone, the same for all three.





PreciselyWhat the demo plots, and Ivrii’s condition on billiard paths uses limits

In the demo all three drums have area |\Omega| = \pi (a disk of radius 1, a square, and a rectangle 4 times as long as it is wide), so the area’s share is \Lambda/4, and “minus the area’s share” plots N(\Lambda) - \Lambda/4, roughly -P\sqrt\Lambda/4\pi: the longer the rim, the lower the curve. The demo’s frequency limit is shown as a multiple of the disk’s lowest frequency, \sqrt{\Lambda}/k_1.
Ivrii’s condition: a billiard path is the path of a ball rolling inside the drum and bouncing off the rim, angle in equal to angle out; it is closed if it comes back to where it started, heading the same way. “Rare” means that if you pick a starting point and a direction at random, the chance of landing on a closed path is zero. Ivrii conjectured that this always holds; it has not been proved. The square and the rectangle in the demo have corners, which his theorem does not cover, but for them the formula can be checked by counting, as in the next fold. The perimeter can be heard in any case, for every drum whose rim is smooth or a polygon, by a smoother way of counting; that is the fold after it.





Proof sketchWeyl’s law for a square, by counting dots uses partial derivatives

Take the square of side s. Its eigenfunctions of -\Delta are \sin(m\pi x/s)\sin(n\pi y/s) for whole numbers m, n \ge 1, with eigenvalues k^2 = (\pi/s)^2(m^2 + n^2); substituting them into the equation checks this, as for the circle on page 3. So N(\Lambda) is the number of dots (m, n), with m, n \ge 1, inside the quarter circle of radius R = s\sqrt\Lambda/\pi.















RR

Give each dot the unit square centered on it. These squares nearly fill the quarter disk, which has area \pi R^2/4. What they miss is a strip of width \tfrac12 along each axis, of area about R/2 each, shaded in the figure; the squares sticking out past the arc and the gaps inside it roughly cancel. So 
N(\Lambda) \approx \frac{\pi R^2}{4} - R = \frac{s^2}{4\pi}\Lambda - \frac{4s}{4\pi}\sqrt\Lambda = \frac{|\Omega|}{4\pi}\Lambda - \frac{P}{4\pi}\sqrt\Lambda .
 In the figure, R = 5.3: there are 17 dots, and the formula gives 16.8. The strips are missing because m = 0 and n = 0 give the zero function, not an eigenfunction: the rim’s condition u = 0 is what costs the perimeter term. Making “roughly cancel” precise is a classical problem about counting lattice points in a circle.





Proof sketchHearing the perimeter of a drum with a smooth or straight-sided rim: a smoother count uses the heat equation and the reflection trick of page 4

N(\Lambda) jumps by one at every eigenvalue, and those jumps can bunch up, which is what Ivrii’s condition controls. A smoother count avoids them. For t > 0 let 
Z(t) = \sum_n e^{-k_n^2 t}.
 Each eigenvalue adds nearly 1 if k_n^2 is much less than 1/t and nearly 0 if it is much more, so Z(t) is roughly N(1/t), with the jumps smoothed out. Like N, Z is determined by the list of eigenvalues.
Z has a physical meaning. Heat spreading on the drumhead, with the rim held at temperature 0, obeys v_t = \Delta v, the drum’s equation with one time derivative instead of two, so each mode now decays like e^{-k_n^2 t} instead of oscillating. Start a unit burst of heat at a point x and let it spread for time t. The temperature it leaves at x itself, added up over all points x of the drum, is Z(t). (Write the burst as a sum of modes, each scaled so that \iint X_n^2\,dA = 1. A burst at x contains mode n in proportion to X_n(x), the same rule as a strike on the drum page; after time t that part has shrunk by e^{-k_n^2 t}, and its temperature at x is again proportional to X_n(x). So the temperature left at x is \sum_n e^{-k_n^2 t}X_n(x)^2, and adding it up over the drum gives \sum_n e^{-k_n^2 t}.) In a short time t heat travels a distance of about \sqrt t, so a burst only feels the rim if it starts within about that distance of it. Kac called this “not feeling the boundary”. Then:

Away from the rim, the burst spreads as on an endless plane, and the temperature it leaves at its starting point is 1/(4\pi t). Adding this up over the drum gives |\Omega|/(4\pi t).
Near a straight piece of rim, at distance r from it, the rim’s condition v = 0 is met by adding a mirror-image burst of opposite sign on the far side of the rim, the odd reflection of the string page. The image is a distance 2r away, and lowers the temperature at x by e^{-r^2/t}/(4\pi t). Adding this up over a strip along the rim, using \int_0^\infty e^{-r^2/t}\,dr = \tfrac12\sqrt{\pi t} for each unit of rim length, gives -P/(8\sqrt{\pi t}).

So, as t \to 0, 
Z(t) = \frac{|\Omega|}{4\pi t} - \frac{P}{8\sqrt{\pi t}} + (\text{terms that stay bounded}).
 Knowing Z, one reads off |\Omega| from the first term and then P from the second. Kac gave this argument in his 1966 paper. Åke Pleijel had already proved the formula for smooth rims in 1954, by another method; Henry McKean and Isadore Singer proved in 1967 the next, constant term, which Kac had conjectured, from an argument that was not a full proof: (1 - h)/6 for a drum with h holes and a smooth rim; and Michiel van den Berg and Sivakolundu Srisatkunarajah proved the formula for polygons in 1988. Unlike N, Z needs no condition on billiard paths, because averaging over a range of eigenvalues smooths out the bunching.


So a round drum can be heard. Of all shapes with the same area, the disk has the shortest rim. This is the isoperimetric inequality: every drum satisfies 
P^2 \ge 4\pi\,|\Omega|,
 with equality only for the disk. Both sides can be heard, for a rim that is smooth or made of straight pieces. So a drum with such a rim that has exactly a disk’s frequencies has the disk’s area and rim length, so P^2 = 4\pi|\Omega|, so it is a disk. Kac pointed this out in section 10 of his 1966 paper: “By pitch alone one can thus determine whether a drum is circular or not!”
But in general, no. Two years before Kac’s paper, John Milnor had found two different shapes with the same frequencies, and Kac said so; but they were 16-dimensional and had no rim. (They are flat tori: 16-dimensional versions of a video-game screen whose edges wrap around, so that leaving on the right brings you back on the left.) For drums in the plane the question stayed open for 26 years. In 1992 Carolyn Gordon, David Webb and Scott Wolpert answered it: no. They found two different polygons with exactly the same frequencies, repeats included: the two drums at the top of this page. Such drums are called isospectral. Since area and rim length can be heard, they must share them, and they do: each is made of seven copies of the same right triangle, with two short sides of length 1, so each has area 3.5 and rim length 6 + 3\sqrt2.
Why do they share every frequency? Cut each drum into its seven triangles. Any mode of drum A can be rebuilt on drum B: fill each of B’s triangles with three triangle-shaped pieces of the mode, taken from A’s triangles, turned or flipped to fit, some with their signs reversed. With the right choice of pieces and signs, they join smoothly across every seam and stay still on B’s rim, so the result is a mode of B, at the same frequency. The construction runs backwards too, so the two drums have exactly the same frequencies, with the same number of modes at each.



DetailsTransplantation: carrying a mode from one drum to the other uses the Laplacian (page 8)

Cut each drum along its seams into its seven triangles. Take any eigenfunction X of drum A, with -\Delta X = k^2 X. On each triangle of drum B, place a sum of three pieces of X, each taken from one of A’s triangles, turned or reflected to fit, and some with a minus sign. Each piece satisfies -\Delta X = k^2 X, so the sum does too, inside each triangle. With the right choice of pieces and signs, the result is zero on B’s rim, and across every seam of B both its values and its slopes match. A function that satisfies the equation on both sides of a line, with values and slopes matching on the line, satisfies it across the line too, a standard fact about this equation. At the points where several seams meet, one more standard fact closes the gap: a solution that stays bounded around a single point, and satisfies the equation everywhere near it except possibly at the point itself, satisfies it there too. So the result is an eigenfunction of B with the same k^2, and so the same frequency. The construction can be reversed, so each eigenvalue has the same multiplicity on both drums.
This argument is called transplantation. It grew out of work of Peter Buser on surfaces in the 1980s and of Pierre Bérard around 1992; the version for drums like these is in a 1994 paper of Buser, John Conway, Peter Doyle and Klaus-Dieter Semmler. The seven formulas, with pictures, are in Cleve Moler’s blog post on transplantation, and in S. J. Chapman’s article, which does the same by folding paper. Gordon, Webb and Wolpert’s own proof used a method of Toshikazu Sunada from 1985 for building isospectral spaces from group theory; Wikipedia has an overview.





DetailsHow the numbers on this page were computed uses matrices, as on page 2

Each drum is covered by a square grid of spacing h, and the Laplacian is replaced by its five-point version: at each grid point, the sum of the four neighbors minus four times the point, divided by h^2. This is the bead model of page 2 in two dimensions. Grid points on the rim are held at zero. The drums’ corners sit on grid points, so whether each point is inside, on the rim, or outside is decided with exact whole-number arithmetic.
At h = 1/40 and h = 1/80 the two drums give the same first twelve eigenvalues k_n^2 of -\Delta to a relative difference of 3\times10^{-14}, which is rounding error. This is expected, as far as I can tell, because the grid lines up with every triangle’s edges, so transplantation works for the grid model too; Moler’s post transplants grid eigenvectors in the same way. Combining the two grids (Richardson extrapolation) gives values within 0.03% of the high-accuracy values in Table 3.1 of Driscoll’s paper, after multiplying his by 4: his drums are twice the size of these. That is a check, not a precise computation: Richardson’s trick assumes the grid error shrinks like h^2, and the drums’ inward-pointing corners slow that down. The page uses Driscoll’s values.
One eigenvalue is known exactly, the ninth, k_9^2. Its mode is, on each triangle, that triangle’s own lowest mode, \sin\pi x\,\sin 2\pi y - \sin 2\pi x\,\sin\pi y in coordinates where the triangle has corners (0,0), (1,0) and (1,1), with its sign flipping across each seam. Substituting gives k_9^2 = \pi^2(1 + 4) = 5\pi^2 = 49.348\ldots, and Driscoll’s value agrees to every digit he gives. On the grid, the ninth eigenvalue equals the grid version of this mode’s eigenvalue to rounding error, a second check.
The scripts are gww.py for the eigenvalues and gww_modes.py for the mode pictures. The corner coordinates are those in Moler’s first post. The mode pictures use the coarser grid h = 1/40, sampled every 0.1.

title: Can you hear the shape of a drum?
text:
What we found
A drum’s spectrum, the eigenvalues of A = -c^2\Delta with the rim held still, tells you its area through Weyl’s law and, for a smooth or straight-sided rim, the length of its rim, which is enough to recognize a round drum. It does not always tell you the shape: Gordon, Webb and Wolpert’s two drums share every frequency, though struck at a point they sound different. The study of what a spectrum says about the shape behind it is called spectral geometry; the last page asks what a spectrum says about music.

title: The Shape of a Sound
text: Pluck a string and you get a note you could hum. Strike a drum and you get a thud. Both are a stretched piece of material, set shaking. So why do they sound so different?

title: The Shape of a Sound
text:
The answer in three steps
1. Everything that vibrates has a set of favorite shapes. A string can swing as one arc, as two halves moving in opposite directions, as three thirds, and so on. Each of these shapes, called a mode, swings at its own frequency.
1×2×3×
2. A pluck sets many of them going at once. What you hear is a mix of the modes’ frequencies: the lowest, called the fundamental, and the overtones above it. They are the stems on the ruler above.
3. Whether that mix sounds like one note depends on how the frequencies line up. If they are all, or very nearly, whole-number multiples of one frequency in the range we hear as pitch, the sound repeats itself at the largest such frequency, many times a second, and the ear hears that repetition rate as the pitch. A string’s modes do exactly that: 1×, 2×, 3×, …. An ideal drumhead’s land at 1×, 1.59×, 2.14×, 2.30×, …: a few fall near a line by chance, but no frequency we hear as pitch fits them all. The sound doesn’t repeat at any rate we hear as pitch, and it dies fast: a thud. Drums with a clear note, such as the timpani (kettledrums), are built so that one set of their modes lands near the lines and the rest are weak or fade fast (page 8).

The idea behind the whole series. Apply Newton’s law to a small piece of an instrument and you get a rule for how its shape is pulled back toward rest: its operator. The shapes that rule only scales up or down are the modes; each swings at its own frequency, and left to ring, the instrument moves as a mix of them. The operator’s spectrum fixes those frequencies, so it decides what the instrument can sound like: on the lines, a note; off the lines, a clang or a thud.

There are no recordings: every note is built from pure tones. The struck and plucked notes fade, at frequencies computed from each instrument's operator (the bass drum's from page 8's ideal drumhead), except the kettledrum's, which are measured, because page 8's simple model gets only halfway to them. The clarinet holds a steady tone with the tube's odd multiples strong and the even ones faint, and the theremin a single steady pure tone. Each lane shows the frequencies on the pitch ruler. The arrangement is ours, after the transcription at flutetunes.com. On a small screen, use Full screen with the phone turned sideways.


The two drums show the series’ answer in miniature. An ideal drumhead’s frequencies are off the lines, so the bass drum booms without a clear pitch; a kettledrum is built so that one set of its modes lands near the lines and the others fade fast, so it plays a note (page 8).

title: The Shape of a Sound
text:
The mathematics in one example
The smallest instrument with more than one mode is two beads on a tight string, with both ends tied. Pull one bead aside and let go, and both beads wobble in a tangled way that never quite repeats. But two ways of starting them are special. Lift both beads together, and they swing together forever, at one frequency. Lift one up and push the other down, and they swing in opposite directions forever, at √3 ≈ 1.73 times that frequency: now the stretch of string between the beads pulls too, so the restoring pull is three times as strong, and a frequency goes as the square root of the pull (page 1).
together: 1×opposite: 1.73×
These two shapes are the beads’ modes, and every motion of the two beads, the tangled one included, is a mix of them, each part swinging at its own frequency. The rule that turns the beads’ heights into the pulls on them is their operator; a mode is a shape that the rule only scales; the numbers that fix the modes’ frequencies form its spectrum. A string, a column of air, a steel bar and a drumhead are the same story with more and more small pieces, each pulled back by its own rule. Page 2 works the two beads out in full, and the spectrum of an operator proves that every free motion is a mix of modes and says where that stops being exact: when a bow or a breath keeps driving the motion, when the swings are large, or when friction mixes the modes.

title: The Shape of a Sound
text:
Did instrument makers know?
Not in these terms. Instruments came first, shaped over centuries by trial and ear; the mathematics came later and explained them, from Mersenne’s laws of vibrating strings (1636) and d’Alembert’s wave equation (1747) to Rayleigh’s The Theory of Sound (1877). Designing an instrument by computing its spectrum is recent: a carillon bell with a major third in its overtones, where traditional bells have a minor third, was designed by computer at the Eindhoven University of Technology for the Eijsbouts bell foundry; the map tells the longer story.

title: The Shape of a Sound
text:
The journey


  The idea
  0What makes a sound a note?When a sound's frequencies are all, or very nearly, whole-number multiples of one frequency, the sound repeats, or nearly repeats, at the largest such frequency, and if that rate is in the range we hear as pitch, the ear hears it as the pitch, even when that frequency itself is missing.▶ The note▶ Without it
  1Why does a fading note stay in tune?A mass on a spring vibrates at one frequency, √(k/m)/2π (k its stiffness, m its mass), and the size of the swing doesn't enter (for small swings), which is why a fading note keeps its pitch.
  2How can a tangled wobble be a few simple motions?With many masses the operator is a table of numbers (a matrix); the shapes it only rescales (its eigenvectors) swing as independent springs, and any motion is a mix of them.
  3Why does a loop of string land exactly on the lines?A loop of string vibrates at exactly 1, 2, 3, … times its lowest frequency, because each wave around it has a whole number of crests and all waves travel at the same speed.
  ★The spectrum of an operatorLeft to ring, an object vibrates as a mix of its modes; the operator fixes their frequencies, and playing sets only how strongly each sounds.
  Instruments
  4Why does a light touch make a string jump an octave?A light touch at the middle drains every mode that moves under the finger and leaves the even modes, which stand still there: a note an octave up.
  5Why is a clarinet almost an octave deeper than a flute?Air in a tube obeys the string's equation with different ends: a tube closed at one end has only odd multiples of its lowest frequency, so a clarinet sounds almost an octave below a flute of the same length and overblows an octave and a fifth higher.▶ Flute-like▶ Clarinet-like
  6Why does a kalimba sound clean?A bar clamped at one end has overtones off whole-number multiples (6.27×, 17.55×), yet a kalimba sounds clean because those overtones die within a fraction of a second (observed, not derived).▶ Kalimba tine
  6bWhere did the harmonica reed's overtones go?Blown, the reed swings just below its own lowest frequency and chops the air into identical puffs, so the steady sound has only whole-number multiples and the reed's off-line overtones are absent from it.▶ Plucked▶ Blown
  7Why do piano tuners stretch octaves?A piano wire's stiffness puts each overtone slightly above its whole-number multiple, so tuners stretch octaves to reduce the beating, a slow wobble in loudness, most at the ends of the keyboard.▶ Exactly 2 : 1▶ Stretched
  8Why does a drum thud?An ideal drumhead's frequencies (1, 1.59, 2.14, … times the lowest) fit no pitch, so a plain drum thuds; on a kettledrum, the air the head pushes pulls one set of modes near 2 : 3 : 4 : 5, a note.

  10Did instruments shape our scales?Two notes sound smooth together when their overtones line up, so instruments with different overtones can favour different scales, as Sethares argues (after Plomp and Levelt).

section: 1 · Newton’s law: the equation of motion
text:
1 · Newton’s law: the equation of motion
Mathematics used: the small-angle approximation and multiplying a table of numbers by a list (explained).
As on page 1, apply Newton’s law to one piece of the instrument, here one bead, and find the force. It will turn out to depend on the bead’s neighbors as well as on the bead itself.
Let u_j be the height of bead j, with N beads, each of mass m, spaced h apart along a string of tension T. Because the loop closes, bead N is next to bead 1, so bead numbers are counted around the ring. (An idealization: the model keeps only the sideways pulls between neighbors, as for a straight string whose two ends are joined.)

  
  
  
  
  
  bead j−1bead jbead j+1
  TTnet pull

1. The string on one side pulls the bead toward its neighbor. The string between beads j and j+1 pulls bead j along itself with force T. That piece of string rises by u_{j+1} - u_j over a distance h, so its slope is (u_{j+1} - u_j)/h. If the string makes a small angle \theta with the horizontal, the upward part of the pull is T\sin\theta; for a small angle \sin\theta \approx \tan\theta (both are about \theta in radians), and \tan\theta is the slope. So the vertical part of the pull is 
T\sin\theta \approx T\tan\theta = \frac{T}{h}\,(u_{j+1} - u_j) .

2. The string on the other side does the same. Its vertical part is 
\frac{T}{h}\,(u_{j-1} - u_j) .

3. The two pulls set the bead’s acceleration. Adding them and setting the total equal to mass times acceleration, 
m\,\ddot u_j = \frac{T}{h}\left(u_{j+1} - 2u_j + u_{j-1}\right).
 The bracket is twice the gap between the average of the two neighbors and bead j itself: a bead sitting above its neighbors is pulled down, one sitting below is pulled up. So each bead is a mass on a spring, except that where its spring pulls it depends on where its neighbors are.
A bead next to a tied-down end is pulled the same way, with that end counting as a neighbor at height 0.
What we assumed. Small slopes, a tension that does not change as the string flexes, point-like beads on a massless string, no friction, and the idealized closed ring described above.

title: How can a tangled wobble be a few simple motions?
text:
2 · The operator
Start with two beads, ends tied. Take two beads on a string whose two ends are tied down, at heights x_1 and x_2. Step 3 of stage 1, with the tied ends as neighbors at height 0, gives 
m\,\ddot x_1 = \frac{T}{h}\,(0 - 2x_1 + x_2), \qquad m\,\ddot x_2 = \frac{T}{h}\,(x_1 - 2x_2 + 0) .
 Each bead’s acceleration depends on where the other bead is: the two equations are tangled together. Collect the two heights into one column x = (x_1, x_2), and the two equations become one, 
\ddot x = -A\,x, \qquad A = \frac{T}{mh}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} .
 The product Ax is worked out row by row: the first entry is the first row, (2, -1), times the column (x_1, x_2), that is \frac{T}{mh}(2x_1 - x_2), which is minus the first equation’s right side divided by m; the second row gives the second equation. Notice that the table is the same read across or down: entry (1, 2) equals entry (2, 1). One stretch of string joins the two beads and feels only the difference of their heights, so moving bead 2 up by one unit pulls bead 1 exactly as hard as moving bead 1 up by one unit pulls bead 2. A table with this property is called symmetric.

  
  
  
  
  x₁x₂ends tied
  
  
  12closed into a ring

The same two beads, closed into a ring. Now join the string’s two ends to each other instead of tying them down. Both of a bead’s neighbors are now the other bead: bead 1 is joined to bead 2 by the string on its left and again by the string on its right. So m\,\ddot x_1 = \frac{T}{h}(x_2 - x_1) + \frac{T}{h}(x_2 - x_1), and the same for bead 2: 
A_{\text{ring}} = \frac{T}{mh}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2 \end{pmatrix} .
 The same beads on the same string, held a different way, give a different operator: how the beads are held is part of the operator.
Any number of beads on a ring. The force on each bead depends on its neighbors, so the rule that turns the shape into the force acts on all the beads at once. Collect the heights into one column u = (u_1, \dots, u_N). The N equations become one, 
\ddot u = -\frac{T}{mh}\,K\,u ,
 where K is a square table of numbers, a matrix, with 2 down its diagonal (top left to bottom right), -1 just above and below it, and -1 in the two corners, because bead 1 and bead N are neighbors. For N = 5, 
K = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 & 0 & 0 & -1\\ -1 & 2 & -1 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & -1 & 2 & -1 & 0\\ 0 & 0 & -1 & 2 & -1\\ -1 & 0 & 0 & -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}.
 Here Ku is the column whose j-th entry is row j of K times u: multiply each entry of row j by the matching entry of u, and add. Row j has 2 in place j and -1 in places j - 1 and j + 1, so (Ku)_j = 2u_j - u_{j-1} - u_{j+1}, which is the bead equation for every bead at once. Each row of K is the row above shifted one place to the right, wrapping around; a matrix with this property is called circulant. The two corner entries are the ring’s boundary condition: they are where the loop closes.

The operator. 
\ddot u = -A\,u, \qquad A = \frac{T}{mh}\,K ,
 a matrix acting on the list of all the beads’ heights, with the ring closed (bead N next to bead 1). In words: on page 1 the operator was one number; here it is a table of numbers, and A\,u is the list of restoring forces per unit mass, reversed.

title: How can a tangled wobble be a few simple motions?
text:
3 · Its spectrum
A mode is a shape that keeps its form while it swings. Most starting shapes change as they move: that is the tangle. Start again with the two tied beads.
1. Two beads: a lucky guess. The two beads are mirror images of each other, which suggests adding and subtracting their equations. With the sum S = x_1 + x_2 and the difference D = x_1 - x_2, adding gives \ddot S = -\frac{T}{mh}\big((2x_1 - x_2) + (2x_2 - x_1)\big) and subtracting gives \ddot D = -\frac{T}{mh}\big((2x_1 - x_2) - (2x_2 - x_1)\big), that is, 
\ddot S = -\frac{T}{mh}\,S, \qquad \ddot D = -\frac{3T}{mh}\,D .
 The tangle has come apart into two independent springs, each the spring of page 1. In S the beads move up and down together, one arch, and the stretch of string between them stays level. In D they move in opposite directions, two arches, and each bead is also pulled by the middle stretch, which is tilted by twice the bead’s height: three times as stiff in all. Going back, x_1 = (S + D)/2 and x_2 = (S - D)/2, so every motion of the two beads is some S-swing plus some D-swing, at the frequencies \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{T/mh} and \sqrt 3 times that. Their ratio, 1 : 1.73, is already off the whole numbers.


x₁x₂

S (together)D (opposite)


In the plane of the two heights, with x_1 across and x_2 up, a mixed motion traces a tangled path; measured along the tilted directions S and D, the same motion is two separate back-and-forth swings.
2. Why the good directions are eigenvectors. Guessing worked because the two beads are mirror images. In general, look for a motion that keeps its shape and only changes its size: x(t) = v\,q(t), a fixed column v times a number q(t) that changes with time. Newton’s law \ddot x = -Ax becomes \ddot q\,v = -q\,Av. At any moment when q \neq 0, this says Av = (-\ddot q/q)\,v: the matrix only rescales v. Since A and v do not change with time, the rescaling factor -\ddot q/q cannot change either; call it \lambda. So 
A v = \lambda\, v, \qquad \ddot q = -\lambda\, q .
 A nonzero column v with Av = \lambda v is called an eigenvector of A, and \lambda its eigenvalue; the list of all the eigenvalues is the matrix’s spectrum. And \ddot q = -\lambda q is page 1’s spring: q = \cos(\omega t + \phi) with \omega^2 = \lambda, so the shape v swings at angular frequency \omega = \sqrt{\lambda}, frequency f = \sqrt{\lambda}/2\pi. The directions in which the beads split into independent springs are exactly the eigenvectors. Since A = \frac{T}{mh}K, the eigenvectors of A are those of the simpler table K: if Kv = s\,v, then Av = \lambda v with \lambda = \frac{T}{mh}\,s.
3. Finding them by hand. For the two tied beads K = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}. Write v = (a, b). The two rows of Kv = s\,v say 2a - b = sa and -a + 2b = sb, that is, b = (2 - s)\,a and a = (2 - s)\,b. Here a \neq 0, since otherwise the first equation gives b = 0 and v would be zero. Putting the first equation into the second, a = (2 - s)^2 a, so (2 - s)^2 = 1: s = 1 or s = 3. For s = 1, b = a: the column (1, 1), the direction S. For s = 3, b = -a: the column (1, -1), the direction D. Check: K(1, 1) = (2 - 1, -1 + 2) = (1, 1) and K(1, -1) = (3, -3) = 3\,(1, -1). The eigenvalues of A are T/mh and 3T/mh, the two springs of step 1.
4. The ring of two beads. For the ring, K_{\text{ring}} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}. Now K_{\text{ring}}(1, 1) = (0, 0): an eigenvector with s = 0. Both beads move up together, nothing stretches, nothing pulls back, and the frequency is 0, so the ring just drifts, with no sound. And K_{\text{ring}}(1, -1) = (4, -4): s = 4, the beads swinging oppositely. Tied ends give eigenvalues proportional to 1 and 3; the ring gives 0 and 4. The way the beads are held changed the spectrum.


  
    
    
  
  
    Together, S
    Opposite, D
    A mix
     close into a ring
    Hear this motion
  
  Slowed down. Tied ends: S swings at 1×, D at 1.73× (√3). Closed into a ring: S has nothing pulling it back, so it only drifts (here it just stays shifted), and D swings at 2×. In the plane on the right, the path of a mix is a tangle, while S and D each run straight along their own tilted line.


5. For any number of beads on a ring, the special shapes are waves around the ring. On a ring no bead is special, so try waves that fit a whole number of times around: v_j = \cos(2\pi jk/N), a wave with k crests. The identity \cos(a + b) + \cos(a - b) = 2\cos a\cos b, with a = 2\pi jk/N and b = 2\pi k/N, gives v_{j+1} + v_{j-1} = 2\cos(2\pi k/N)\,v_j, so 
\begin{aligned}
(Kv)_j &= 2v_j - v_{j+1} - v_{j-1} \\
&= \big(2 - 2\cos(2\pi k/N)\big)\,v_j \\
&= 4\sin^2\!\Big(\frac{\pi k}{N}\Big)\,v_j ,
\end{aligned}
 using 1 - \cos 2x = 2\sin^2 x. The same holds for v_j = \sin(2\pi jk/N). These are the shapes the mode buttons play. At the beads, a wave with N - k crests looks exactly like one with k crests (the cosine is the same and the sine changes sign), so the different eigenvalues come from k = 0, 1, \dots up to N/2, rounded down, and each one from k = 1 up to just below N/2 has two eigenvectors, a cosine and a sine. (At k = 0, and at k = N/2 when N is even, the sine is zero at every bead, so only the cosine is left.) A wave with more crests bends more sharply from bead to bead, so each bead is pulled back harder and the wave swings faster.

The spectrum. Eigenvectors: the waves \cos(2\pi jk/N) and \sin(2\pi jk/N) with k crests. Eigenvalues of A: 
\lambda_k = \frac{4T}{mh}\,\sin^2\!\Big(\frac{\pi k}{N}\Big), \qquad f_k = \frac{\sqrt{\lambda_k}}{2\pi} = \frac{1}{\pi}\sqrt{\frac{T}{mh}}\,\sin\frac{\pi k}{N} .
 In words: mode k sounds at \sin(\pi k/N)/\sin(\pi/N) times mode 1.

In the 1730s Daniel Bernoulli studied systems like this, weights strung along a flexible thread and a hanging chain, and came to believe that every vibration is built from such simple motions; in 1753 he put this forward as a general principle. For the beads it is a theorem, and writing a motion as a sum of these waves is the discrete Fourier transform.



ProofEvery motion is a sum of modes uses linear algebra

The matrix A is symmetric, so the hub’s Result applies word for word: its eigenvectors form a perpendicular basis, each amount obeys its own mass-on-a-spring equation, and the starting shape and velocity fix the motion. The one fact specific to the ring is that the eigenvalues are nonnegative: u \cdot Ku = \sum_j u_j(2u_j - u_{j+1} - u_{j-1}) = \sum_j (u_{j+1} - u_j)^2 \ge 0, by regrouping the terms around the ring, and for an eigenvector of A this gives \lambda\,(u\cdot u) = \frac{T}{mh}\,u\cdot Ku \ge 0.





PreciselyThe same waves, written with complex numbers uses complex numbers

With Euler’s formula e^{ix} = \cos x + i\sin x, the cosine and sine waves combine into v_j = e^{2\pi i jk/N} for k = 0, 1, \dots, N - 1 (here i is the imaginary unit and j the bead number). Then (Kv)_j = \big(2 - e^{2\pi ik/N} - e^{-2\pi ik/N}\big)v_j = 4\sin^2(\pi k/N)\,v_j in one line. These N waves are the basis vectors of the discrete Fourier transform, and they are eigenvectors of every circulant matrix, not only this one. Combined with the time factor e^{\mp i\omega t}, the waves with k and N - k crests travel around the ring in opposite directions.

text:
4 · On the spectrum diagram
The stems are the frequencies f_k from the result box, as multiples of mode 1’s, the slowest wave that swings back and forth: mode k stands at \sin(\pi k/N)/\sin(\pi/N). In the demo at the top, each stem’s height is how much of that mode the current motion contains; below, every mode is drawn equally tall. Apart from mode 1 itself, they generally miss the lines. With 8 beads, as the demo starts, the modes sit at 1×, 1.85×, 2.41× and 2.61×. Raise the number of beads and the low stems close in on the lines: with 24 beads, modes 2 and 3 are within 2.5% of 2× and 3×. The high modes stay far off.


  
  
  Each mode's frequency as a multiple of mode 1's, every mode drawn equally tall: 8 beads (top), 24 beads (bottom). Adding beads pulls the low modes onto the lines; the high ones stay off.

title: How can a tangled wobble be a few simple motions?
text:
5 · What we hear
The jangle is a mix of pure tones. Pluck one bead and the starting shape is not a wave; but it is a sum of waves, and each wave swings at its own frequency. So the plucked ring sounds all those frequencies at once. They sit off the lines, so they don’t fuse into one note: a jangle. Start the ring in one wave’s shape and only that one frequency sounds: a pure tone. The clean tones were in the jangle all along, as its eigenvectors.
Any motion of the ring is a sum of modes, u(t) = \sum_k a_k\, v^{(k)}\cos(2\pi f_k t + \phi_k), each swinging at its own frequency as if it were alone (the proof is in the fold above). The demo’s sound is exactly this sum: it adds the modes’ frequencies f_k, with mode 1 set to 196 Hz, each as strong as the motion contains it.
Almost whole numbers. A long wave, with few crests, spreads over many beads, and to it the beads look like a smooth string; its frequency grows in step with its number of crests, almost exactly as whole numbers do. A short wave, with crests only a bead or two apart, feels the gaps between the beads, and its frequency falls behind. That is why the low stems sit near the lines and close in as you add beads, while the high ones stay off.



PreciselyHow near to whole numbers uses the sine function

Mode k has frequency proportional to \sin(\pi k/N), which is not proportional to k: the beads are not exactly harmonic. For small k, \sin(\pi k/N) \approx \pi k/N, so the low modes are nearly harmonic, and the ratio \sin(\pi k/N)/\sin(\pi/N) tends to k as N grows. The modes near k = N/2 stay far from the whole-number grid: for an even number of beads the largest ratio is 1/\sin(\pi/N) (slightly less for an odd number), and for any number of beads it is about N/\pi once there are many, not N/2. A mode can land on a line by coincidence: with 6 beads, the top mode sits at exactly 2×.

title: How can a tangled wobble be a few simple motions?
text:
What we found
With many masses the operator is a matrix, and its eigenvectors are the directions in which the motion splits into independent springs: for two tied beads, together and opposite, at 1 and √3 times; for N beads on a ring, waves with \lambda_k = \frac{4T}{mh}\sin^2(\pi k/N). Any motion, even a tangle, is a mix of these springs, and on the spectrum diagram the low ones sit near the lines but not on them.

title: What makes a sound a note?
text:
The pitch ruler
The stems under the wave are the note’s frequencies, drawn as multiples of 220 Hz: 1×, 2×, 3×, …. Those whole-number multiples are the lines of the pitch ruler, and every page of this series puts an instrument on it: stems on the pitch ruler, one per mode, make the spectrum diagram that stage 4 of every instrument page draws. A note’s frequencies sit on the lines. Take away the 1× stem and the rest still sit on lines of the same ruler, so the pitch is still 220 Hz. The component at the repetition rate itself is called the fundamental. Hearing the pitch without it is called the missing fundamental effect, and it is why a deep voice keeps its pitch over an ordinary telephone line, which cannot carry sounds below about 300 Hz.
Open “Mix your own” and try the presets. The stems’ heights change, and so does the sound’s color, its timbre, but the pitch stays put as long as the base frequency does. Keep only 2×, 4×, 6× and 8×, and the sound repeats twice as often: the base becomes 440 Hz, and the pitch jumps up an octave.

title: What makes a sound a note?
text:
How it works
A note is a pattern that repeats. Sound is air pressure rising and falling. When the pattern repeats, you hear a note, and its pitch is the repetition rate, measured in hertz. This holds for rates in the range where we hear pitch, from a few dozen to a few thousand times a second (for a recognizable melody, roughly 30 Hz to 4 or 5 kHz: Pressnitzer and colleagues measured the lower limit; the upper one is the traditional limit, which Oxenham and colleagues revisit). Much slower repetition is heard as a rhythm. Middle C, called C4, repeats about 262 times a second.
Every repeating sound is a chord on the lines. A pure tone is a single sine-shaped wave, the sound of a tuning fork. Any repeating pattern can be built from pure tones at 1, 2, 3, … times its repetition rate, and from no others; this is Fourier’s theorem, and page 3 shows where it comes from. These tones are the sound’s partials, and the one at the repetition rate itself is the fundamental. The repetition rate sets the pitch, whether or not the fundamental is actually there; the partials’ strengths set the timbre.
In symbols: sound is a pressure signal p(t). It is periodic with period P if p(t + P) = p(t) for every t; take P to be the shortest such time. The pitch is the repetition rate f = 1/P, for rates in the range where we hear pitch. Any periodic signal that is not too wild (continuous and made of smooth pieces is plenty) is the sum of its Fourier series: with f = 1/P, 
p(t) = \sum_{n \ge 0} b_n \cos(2\pi n f t + \phi_n) .
 The n = 0 term is a constant, the average pressure, usually zero. The possible frequencies nf are fixed by the period alone, and a given sound may use only some of them: a pure tone uses only f. The amplitudes b_n and the phases \phi_n carry everything else about the sound’s shape, and the ear is mostly insensitive to the phases.

A note, in symbols. A sound that repeats every P seconds contains only the frequencies f, 2f, 3f, \dots with f = 1/P: whole-number multiples of its repetition rate, which is its pitch.




Reader questionIs a musical note one frequency?

No. A note is a sound whose pressure repeats every P seconds, and its pitch is the repetition rate f = 1/P. By the Fourier series above, its components can only be at f, 2f, 3f, \dots, and usually several are present at once. The repetition rate sets the pitch, whether or not a component at f itself is present, and the weights b_n set the timbre: a piano C4 and a violin C4 share f and differ in their b_n. So a note corresponds to a period, not to a single frequency.


Why whole numbers matter. Turn it around. If something vibrates at several frequencies at once, its sound repeats only when they are all whole-number multiples of one common frequency. For two tones, the ratio of their frequencies must be a fraction, such as 3/2; the sound then repeats every 2 cycles of the lower tone. The reason is short. Write the ratio in lowest terms, f_2/f_1 = j/k, and wait P = k/f_1 seconds. In that time the lower tone completes f_1P = k whole cycles and the upper one f_2P = j whole cycles, so both are back where they started, and the sum begins again: it repeats every k cycles of the lower tone. A ratio like 1.59, which is 159/100, repeats only every 100 cycles of the lower tone, far too slowly to hear as one pitch. Try it:


  ▶ 2 : 1▶ 3 : 2▶ 1.59 : 1 (a drum)Play the slider's ratio
  Ratio2.00×
  
  
  Gray ticks mark cycles of the lower tone. At 2 : 1 the sum repeats every cycle; at 3 : 2 every two; at 1.59 : 1, which is 159/100, it lines up only after 100 cycles of the lower tone, far too slowly to hear as one pitch.


Not every instrument is exact. Frequencies very near whole-number multiples still sound like one note: a piano’s are slightly off, as page 7 shows, and it still plays notes. So the rule this series tests every instrument against reads: frequencies at, or very near, whole-number multiples of one frequency in the range we hear as pitch make a note.
Where the frequencies come from. This page took the frequencies as given. Every later page computes them. Newton’s law, applied to a small piece of the instrument, gives a rule that turns the instrument’s shape into the force pulling it back, the instrument’s operator, and the operator’s special numbers, its eigenvalues, give the frequencies. Page 1 sets this up with the simplest example, one mass on a spring, and page 2 shows why the eigenvalues are the whole story. Whether the frequencies land on the lines of the pitch ruler is the first test of whether the instrument plays a note; pages 6 and 6b show what the frequencies alone do not decide.



ProofThe converse: if two tones repeat together, their ratio is a fraction, and the shortest period uses cosines and divisibility

Let s(t) = \cos(2\pi f_1 t) + \cos(2\pi f_2 t) with 0 < f_1 < f_2.
If the ratio is rational, s is periodic. Write f_2/f_1 = j/k in lowest terms and put P = k/f_1. Then f_1P = k and f_2P = j are whole numbers, so both cosines return to their starting values after time P, and s(t+P) = s(t).
If s is periodic, the ratio is rational. Suppose s(t+P) = s(t) for all t, with P > 0. At t = 0 this gives s(P) = s(0) = 2. A sum of two cosines equals 2 only when both cosines equal 1, so \cos(2\pi f_1P) = \cos(2\pi f_2P) = 1, which means f_1P and f_2P are whole numbers. So f_2/f_1 = (f_2P)/(f_1P) is a ratio of whole numbers. Since f_2/f_1 = j/k, we have k\,(f_2P) = j\,(f_1P), so k divides j\,(f_1P); as j and k share no factor, k divides the whole number f_1P. So every period is a multiple of k/f_1, and k/f_1 is the shortest one.
The shortest period k/f_1 grows with the denominator k. A ratio like 1.59 = 159/100 is rational, but its pattern repeats only every 100 cycles of the lower tone, far too slowly for the ear to hear as one pitch. How the ear decides what counts as “simple enough”, and how near to whole-number multiples is near enough, are questions of perception, not mathematics; see pitch.

title: What makes a sound a note?
text:
What we found
Frequencies at whole-number multiples of one frequency add up to a sound that repeats at that rate, and the ear hears the rate as the pitch, even when that frequency is missing. Every later page computes an instrument’s frequencies and puts them on the pitch ruler: on or very near the lines, a note; off them, a clang or a thud. Page 1 starts with the simplest thing that vibrates.

text:
1 · Newton’s law: the equation of motion
Mathematics used: partial derivatives, an integral over a cross-section, cosh and sinh, and a 2×2 determinant (all explained).
A string is held straight by tension. A tine is under no tension at all: it springs back because steel resists being bent. To find the force behind that, we apply Newton’s law, mass times acceleration equals force, to one thin slice of the tine.
Let u(x, t) be the tine’s height at distance x from the clamp at time t; subscripts are partial derivatives, so u_{xx} is the curvature, how sharply the tine bends. The tine is steel of Young’s modulus E (how stiff the steel is) and density \rho, with cross-section area S.
1. Bending stretches the outside and squeezes the inside. Bend the bar. Fibers on the outside of the curve stretch and fibers on the inside compress, while a middle line, the neutral axis, keeps its length.

  
  
  
  
  stretched (y > 0)compressed (y < 0)
  neutral axis, y = 0

For a gentle bend, a fiber at height y above the neutral axis is stretched by the fraction -y\,u_{xx}: its distance from the axis times how fast the bar turns per unit length. (The minus sign: where u_{xx} < 0 the bar bends down, and its top side, y > 0, is on the outside of the curve and stretched.) By Hooke’s law the fiber then carries the stress (force per area) -E\,y\,u_{xx}. Summed over the cross-section, these forces cancel, which is what places the neutral axis through the middle (the centroid) of the cross-section; but their turning effects do not cancel. Add them up over the small bits of area dA of the cross-section S, each pulling with stress times dA at lever arm y; the total is the bending moment 
\begin{aligned}
M &= -\int_S y\,(-E\,y\,u_{xx})\,dA = E\,u_{xx}\int_S y^2\,dA \\
&= EI\,u_{xx} .
\end{aligned}
 The number I = \int_S y^2\,dA, the second moment of area, says how the cross-section’s shape resists bending. For a rectangle of width w and thickness h, the strip at height y has area w\,dy, so I = \int_{-h/2}^{h/2} y^2\,w\,dy = wh^3/12; for a round wire of diameter d, I = \pi d^4/64.
2. A change in bending moment along the tine is a sideways force. A moment turns a slice but cannot lift it. Each face of a slice also carries a vertical force, the shear force V. The conventions: M is the moment on a face that bends the slice into an upward curve, counterclockwise on the right face and clockwise on the left; V is the upward force on the right face, and the left face feels the same force downward.

  
  
  
  
  
  
  MM + dM
  VV + dVdx

We neglect the slice’s resistance to being spun, its rotational inertia, which is accurate when the bar is thin compared with the length of its bending waves; then the turning effects on the slice must balance. Taking them about the left face, the shear on the right face times the lever arm dx cancels the change in moment: V\,dx + dM = 0, so 
V = -M_x = -EI\,u_{xxx} .

3. Newton’s law on the slice. The vertical forces on the two faces do not balance: their difference, V(x + dx) - V(x) = V_x\,dx, accelerates the slice’s mass \rho S\,dx. So 
\rho S\,u_{tt} = V_x = -EI\,u_{xxxx} .
 Dividing by the mass per length \rho S, this is the Euler–Bernoulli beam equation, u_{tt} = -\kappa^2 u_{xxxx} with \kappa^2 = EI/\rho S.
What we assumed. Small slopes; a uniform bar; no rotational inertia of the slices (Rayleigh’s correction for it adds a small term that matters only for thick bars and high modes); no shear deformation of the slices (Timoshenko’s correction); a tine clamped at exactly one point; and no damping or sound radiation: in this model every mode rings forever, and how fast the overtone dies is taken from measurement (stage 5).

title: Why does a kalimba sound clean?
text:
2 · The operator
Read the beam equation as a rule: take the tine’s shape, differentiate it four times along the tine, and multiply by \kappa^2. That is minus the restoring force per unit mass, the tine’s operator A = \kappa^2\,d^4/dx^4, and the equation reads u_{tt} = -Au.
The ends. At the base the tine is held down, so it can neither move nor tilt: u = 0 and u_x = 0. A bar held this way at one end and free at the other is called a cantilever. At the free tip nothing pushes or bends the bar, so both the moment and the shear force vanish: u_{xx} = 0 and u_{xxx} = 0. That is two conditions at each end, four in all, as a fourth-order operator needs; they are part of the operator, as the tied ends were for the string.

The tine’s operator. 
\begin{gathered}
u_{tt} = -A\,u, \qquad A = \kappa^2\,\frac{d^4}{dx^4}, \\
\kappa^2 = \frac{EI}{\rho S},
\end{gathered}
 with u = u_x = 0 at the clamp and u_{xx} = u_{xxx} = 0 at the tip. In words: the force per unit mass pulling each point back is the fourth derivative of the shape, times a constant set by the steel and the cross-section. The string’s operator was -c^2\,d^2/dx^2: two derivatives instead of four.

What four derivatives do. Squeeze a shape into half the length, and every rate of change along it doubles. A string’s pull depends on its curvature, how sharply it bends, a rate of change of a rate of change: 2 × 2 = 4 times harder. A tine’s push depends on how that curvature itself changes along the tine, twice over: 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16 times harder. Both of the tine’s surprises in stage 5 come from this.

title: Why does a kalimba sound clean?
text:
3 · Its spectrum
A mode is a shape X(x) that the operator only rescales, A X = \lambda X. Such a shape swings as X(x)\cos\omega t with \omega = \sqrt\lambda, at the frequency f = \sqrt\lambda/2\pi. The list of all the eigenvalues \lambda is the operator’s spectrum. For the tine, the mode equation is 
\kappa^2 X'''' = \lambda X .

1. Which shapes does the operator only rescale? Write \lambda = \kappa^2\beta^4, so that X'''' = \beta^4 X: four derivatives give back the shape, times \beta^4. The number \beta plays the role of the string’s wavenumber. Four functions do this: \cos\beta x, \sin\beta x, \cosh\beta x and \sinh\beta x, where \cosh y = (e^y + e^{-y})/2 and \sinh y = (e^y - e^{-y})/2 are the hyperbolic functions. Differentiating the definitions, (\cosh y)' = \sinh y and (\sinh y)' = \cosh y, with no sign changes, so the hyperbolic pair gives back \beta^4 times itself after four derivatives, just as \cos and \sin do after their sign flips cancel; multiplying out the definitions also gives \cosh^2 y - \sinh^2 y = 1, and \cosh 0 = 1, \sinh 0 = 0. So X is a combination of the four, with four unknown constants, and the four end conditions are four equations for them.
2. Hold the clamped end still. X(0) = 0 and X'(0) = 0 leave two constants: 
\begin{aligned}
X = {}&a\,(\cos\beta x - \cosh\beta x) \\
&+ b\,(\sin\beta x - \sinh\beta x) .
\end{aligned}

3. Leave the free tip unbent and unpushed. Differentiating, and dropping the common factors \beta^2 and \beta^3, the conditions X''(L) = 0 and X'''(L) = 0 read, with the shorthand c_1 = \cos\beta L, s_1 = \sin\beta L, c_2 = \cosh\beta L, s_2 = \sinh\beta L: 
\begin{gathered}
-(c_1 + c_2)\,a - (s_1 + s_2)\,b = 0, \\
(s_1 - s_2)\,a - (c_1 + c_2)\,b = 0 .
\end{gathered}

4. When is there a mode? Two equations pa + qb = 0 and ra + sb = 0 have a solution other than a = b = 0 exactly when ps - qr = 0, the determinant (solve the first for a and substitute into the second). Here 
\begin{aligned}
&(c_1 + c_2)^2 + (s_1 + s_2)(s_1 - s_2) \\
&\quad = c_1^2 + s_1^2 + 2c_1c_2 + c_2^2 - s_2^2 \\
&\quad = 2 + 2c_1c_2 = 0,
\end{aligned}
 using c_1^2 + s_1^2 = 1 and c_2^2 - s_2^2 = 1. So the tine has a mode exactly when 
\cos\beta L\,\cosh\beta L = -1 .

5. Find the roots. Since \cosh\beta L grows fast, \cos\beta L must be close to 0, so \beta L sits near (n - \tfrac12)\pi, closer and closer as n grows. Solved numerically, the roots are \beta L = 1.8751,\ 4.6941,\ 7.8548,\ 10.9955, \dots; the first is the furthest from its estimate, \pi/2 \approx 1.571, because the clamp and the free tip shift it most.

The tine’s spectrum. The modes are X_n = \cosh\beta_n x - \cos\beta_n x - \sigma_n(\sinh\beta_n x - \sin\beta_n x), which is step 2 with a = -1 and b = \sigma_n = (\sinh\beta_nL - \sin\beta_nL)/(\cosh\beta_nL + \cos\beta_nL), from the second equation of step 3 (the first gives (c_1 + c_2)/(s_1 + s_2), the same number at every root, by the mode condition). Their eigenvalues are \lambda_n = \kappa^2\beta_n^4, and their frequencies are 
f_n = \frac{\sqrt{\lambda_n}}{2\pi} = \frac{\kappa\,\beta_n^2}{2\pi} = \frac{\kappa\,(\beta_nL)^2}{2\pi L^2} .
 Since f_n \propto (\beta_nL)^2, the frequency ratios are 1 : 6.27 : 17.55 : 34.39 : \cdots, growing like {(2n-1)^2}: off the whole numbers.

Compare pinned ends. A bar held in place at both ends but free to pivot has u = u_{xx} = 0 at each end. Then the shapes \sin(n\pi x/L) satisfy all four conditions, four derivatives multiply them by (n\pi/L)^4, and the ratios are 1 : 4 : 9 : 16: whole numbers. If every root of the clamped–free tine sat exactly at (n - \tfrac12)\pi, its ratios would be the whole numbers 1 : 9 : 25 too; the shift of the first root is what puts them off the lines.



ProofWhy the eigenvalues are real and positive, and the modes perpendicular uses integration by parts

The operator d^4/dx^4 with these four conditions is symmetric, by integrating by parts four times (the boundary terms all vanish), so its eigenvalues are real and its eigenfunctions perpendicular, as on the circle; with the right domain it is also self-adjoint. Integrating by parts twice gives \int_0^L X\,X''''\,dx = \int_0^L (X'')^2\,dx, so no eigenvalue is negative, and zero is ruled out because X'' = 0 with a clamped base forces X = 0. That is why \beta is a real, positive number.

title: Why does a kalimba sound clean?
text:
5 · What we hear
Why the note still sounds clean. You might guess the overtone is too quiet to hear. It isn’t. In how far the tine swings, the overtone is tiny; but the body hears the push on the bridge, not the swing, and in that push the overtone starts strong (fold below). That strong start is the click at the beginning of each note. What keeps the note clean is that the overtone dies within a fraction of a second, while the fundamental rings on, and the fundamental left on its own is a clean note. That fast decay is observed, not derived: the model of stages 1 to 3 has no damping, and the page takes the decay from measurement. The acoustician D. M. F. Chapman found exactly this pattern on a real kalimba: one dominant overtone, at 5.9 to 6.8 times the fundamental, which dies away so fast that it is heard only at the instant the note starts. With the box ticked, the off-line overtones keep ringing, and the same tine clangs like a bell.



Step-by-step derivationHow strongly a pluck at the tip excites each mode uses integration by parts

Chapman measured the tines of one kalimba, a Hugh Tracey pentatonic, and found one dominant overtone at 5.9 to 6.8 times the fundamental, near the ideal 6.27, dying away quickly after the attack. A real tine is clamped a little behind the bridge and rests on the bridge partway along, rather than being perfectly clamped at one point, and he found that the measured ratios depend on how the bridge divides the tine’s length, which is one reason they spread. The steps below compute, for the ideal tine, how much of each mode a pluck starts. In short: in displacement, the second mode starts at only 2.5% of the first; but at the clamp, where in this ideal model the tine presses on the bridge, it starts at about 16% of the first in bending moment and 55% in shear force. Those are two different measures of the push on the bridge, not a range of uncertainty.

The pluck shape. Before release, a push F at the tip holds the tine still in a bent shape u_0, so the bar’s restoring force balances the push.
Split it into modes. Write u_0 = \sum_n a_n X_n, with each mode scaled so that \int_0^L X_n^2\,dx = L. Inside the tine nothing pushes, so EI\,u_0'''' = 0 there; the push enters only at the tip, as the shear force there. Now compute \int_0^L EI\,u_0\,X_n''''\,dx in two ways. First, EI\,X_n'''' = \rho S\,\omega_n^2X_n (the mode equation), and the modes are perpendicular, so only the a_n term survives: the integral is \rho S L\,\omega_n^2\,a_n. Second, integrate by parts four times to move the derivatives onto u_0, as in the proof fold above. Inside, EI\,u_0'''' = 0; at the clamp both u_0 and X_n vanish with their slopes; at the tip X_n'' = X_n''' = 0 and u_0'' = 0. The one term left is the tip’s shear force times X_n(L), which is F\,X_n(L). So \rho S L\,\omega_n^2\,a_n = F\,X_n(L). This is page 1’s spring again: mode n is a spring of stiffness proportional to \omega_n^2, pushed with a force proportional to its value at the tip, and it gives way by force over stiffness.
Tip values. Use the modes in the standard form of the spectrum box above, with \sigma_n about 0.734 and 1.018 for the first two modes. Written this way, each mode already has \int_0^L X_n^2\,dx = L, and its tip value is \pm2 for every n (a known property of clamped–free modes, easily confirmed numerically). So a_n \propto 1/\omega_n^2, and a_2/a_1 = 1/6.27^2 \approx 2.5\%.
Forces. In this model the tine is clamped right at the bridge, so the forces at the clamp are the forces on the bridge. The bending moment at the clamp is EI\,u_{xx} there, and the shear force EI\,u_{xxx} there (up to sign). From the standard form, X_n''(0) = 2\beta_n^2 and X_n'''(0) = -2\sigma_n\beta_n^3. Multiplying by a_n \propto 1/\omega_n^2 \propto 1/\beta_n^4, the second mode’s moment at the clamp is (\beta_1/\beta_2)^2 = (1.875/4.694)^2 \approx 16\% of the first’s, and its shear force (\sigma_2/\sigma_1)(\beta_1/\beta_2) \approx 1.39 \times 0.40 \approx 55\%.



A plucked tine moves as the sum of its modes, u = \sum_n a_n X_n(x)\cos(2\pi f_n t + \phi_n), each mode fading at its own rate. The demo’s sound is made exactly this way: it adds up the first five modes at the frequencies of stage 3, each starting with its shear-force strength from the fold above (55% for the second mode), as in stage 4. The fundamental fades over a couple of seconds and the overtones within a small fraction of that; those fading rates are an illustrative choice consistent with Chapman’s observation, not computed. Tick the box and every mode fades as slowly as the fundamental.
Overtones off the lines. Higher modes bend in shorter humps, and for a tine shorter humps push back much harder, so the frequencies grow like the square of the mode number instead of the number itself. Where exactly they land is set by the four end conditions: pinned ends would give the whole numbers 1, 4, 9, 16, but a tine is clamped at one end and free at the other, and its spectrum is 1, 6.27, 17.55, …, off the lines.
Half the length, two octaves up. The result box says f_n = \kappa(\beta_nL)^2/(2\pi L^2), and the numbers \beta_nL do not depend on the length: so a tine’s frequency goes as one over its length squared. Half the length gives 4 times the frequency, two octaves, where a string, with f \propto 1/L, rises only an octave. That is why the low tines in the demo are not twice as long as the high ones an octave up. Kalimba makers tune a tine by sliding it over the bridge to change its free length (Kalimba Magic), and the 1/L^2 makes a small slide go a long way.

title: Why does a kalimba sound clean?
text:
What we found
A tine is a bar clamped at one end, with the operator A = \kappa^2\,d^4/dx^4, and its spectrum, from \cos\beta L\cosh\beta L = -1, puts the overtones at 6.27 and 17.55 times the lowest, off the whole-number multiples: four derivatives spread the frequencies like the squares, and the clamped and free ends keep them off the whole numbers. A kalimba still sounds clean because those overtones die within a fraction of a second, which is observed on real kalimbas, not derived here. The next page blows the same kind of bar instead of plucking it.

The tine’s operator family. Harmonica reeds and the teeth of a music box’s steel comb are also bars clamped at one end and free at the other: the same operator with the same ends, so the series puts them in the kalimba’s operator family.

title: Why does a drum thud?
text:
← 7 Piano · The Shape of a Sound · Spectrum of an operator · Map · 9 Drum shape →
The short answer: an ideal, uniform head has its frequencies off the lines, so it thuds; drums with a clear note, such as the timpani (kettledrums), are built so that one set of modes lands near the lines and the rest are weak or fade fast (stage 5).
Listen first: tap the head anywhere, then tap dead center and compare.

title: Why does a drum thud?
section: 1 · Newton’s law: the equation of motion
text:
1 · Newton’s law: the equation of motion
Mathematics used: partial derivatives, integrals over an area, the divergence theorem and polar coordinates (quoted), and Bessel functions (described, computed numerically).
Here is where the drum’s frequencies come from. Apply Newton’s law, mass times acceleration equals force, to one small patch of the drumhead. The steps are the string’s, with one more dimension.
1. One small patch. Let u(x, y, t) be the height of the head above its rest position at the point (x, y) at time t; subscripts are partial derivatives. The head has mass \sigma per unit area, and its tension T is a force per unit length of any cut through it. Take any small patch D of the head. Its mass is the sum of \sigma\,dA over its tiny area pieces dA; the double integral \iint_D below means exactly that, adding up over all the small pieces dA of D. So Newton’s law for its up-and-down motion reads 
\iint_D \sigma\,u_{tt}\,dA = \text{net force on the patch}.

2. The pull across its edge. Along each short piece ds of the patch’s edge, the sheet outside pulls with force T\,ds, along the surface and outward. If the head makes a small angle \theta with the horizontal there, the upward part of that pull is T\sin\theta\,ds; for a small angle \sin\theta \approx \tan\theta (both are about \theta in radians), and \tan\theta is the slope. So the upward part is T\,\partial_n u\,ds, where \partial_n u is the slope of the head in the outward direction across the edge. This is the string’s step, with the slope taken across the edge.


    
      
      
      
      
      
      
      patch DT ds
    
    Tension pulls outward all around the edge. Where the sheet bulges, the pulls tilt and their vertical parts add up to a net force, which step 3 below works out.
  

3. Add the pulls around the edge. The symbol \oint_{\partial D} means adding up all the way around the edge \partial D of the patch. Adding up the pulls around the edge turns into adding up one quantity over the inside of the patch. That is the divergence theorem, quoted here, applied to the slope vector (u_x, u_y): its outward part across the edge is \partial_n u, and its divergence is u_{xx} + u_{yy}. So 
T\oint_{\partial D} \partial_n u\,ds = T\iint_D \Delta u\,dA .
 The quantity \Delta u = u_{xx} + u_{yy}, the Laplacian, adds the second derivatives in the two directions across the sheet. In one dimension a patch is a segment, its edge is its two endpoints, and this step is the fundamental theorem of calculus, u_x(b) - u_x(a) = \int_a^b u_{xx}\,dx: the string’s force again.
4. Newton’s law, at every point. Steps 1 to 3 give \iint_D \sigma\,u_{tt}\,dA = T\iint_D \Delta u\,dA. This holds for every patch, however small, so the two integrands are equal at every point: 
\sigma\,u_{tt} = T\,\Delta u .
 In words: on a string, tension pulls each point toward the average height of its two neighbors; on a sheet it pulls each point toward the average height of all the points around it, and \Delta u measures how far a point sits below that average.
What we assumed. Small slopes; a tension that is the same everywhere and does not change as the head moves; no bending stiffness; no air; and no damping and no sound radiation, so the model’s modes never fade, while a real head loses its energy to the air quickly. The air matters for real drums, as the timpani paragraph in stage 5 says.

title: Why does a drum thud?
text:
2 · The operator
Dividing by the mass per unit area \sigma puts the equation in the series’ form u_{tt} = -A\,u: the force per unit mass is a fixed rule applied to the head’s shape, and that rule is the drum’s operator. The rim completes it: the rim is clamped, so u = 0 there. This is the drum’s boundary condition.

The drum’s operator. 
u_{tt} = -A\,u, \qquad A = -c^2\,\Delta,
 with c^2 = T/\sigma, acting on shapes of the head that are zero on the rim. In words: tension pulls each point toward the average of its surroundings, and the rim holds still.

title: Why does a drum thud?
text:
3 · Its spectrum
A mode is a shape X that the operator only rescales: A X = \lambda X, with the number \lambda called its eigenvalue (an eigenvalue of A, constant included). Released in that shape, the head keeps it and swings as X\cos\omega t, with \omega = \sqrt{\lambda}, at the frequency f = \sqrt{\lambda}/2\pi. The list of all the eigenvalues is the operator’s spectrum. Writing \lambda = c^2k^2, the mode condition is 
-\Delta X = k^2 X
 inside the drum, with X = 0 on the rim and \omega = ck. For a round drum of radius a, it can be solved by splitting it into a problem around the center and a problem outward from it, a separation of variables.
1. A round drum calls for distance and angle. Measure position by the distance r from the center and the angle \theta. In these coordinates the Laplacian reads 
\Delta X = X_{rr} + \frac1r X_r + \frac{1}{r^2}X_{\theta\theta}.
 This is a standard change of variables, quoted here; it follows from the chain rule (Laplace operator in polar coordinates). The X_r/r term is there because circles around the center grow longer as r grows.
2. Split the shape into an around part and an outward part. Try a shape that is a function of r times a function of \theta, X = R(r)\,\Theta(\theta). Substituting into -\Delta X = k^2X and multiplying by r^2/(R\Theta) gives 
\frac{r^2R'' + rR' + k^2r^2R}{R} = -\frac{\Theta''}{\Theta}.
 The left side depends only on r, the right only on \theta. Change \theta alone: the left side can’t change, so neither can the right. So both equal one constant.
3. Around the center: the loop of page 3. Going once around the drum must bring \Theta back to itself, so -\Theta'' = m^2\Theta with \Theta repeating every turn. This is exactly the loop’s eigenvalue problem from the circle page: m is a whole number and \Theta = \cos m\theta or \sin m\theta. A mode with m \ge 1 has m straight still lines through the center, like spokes.
4. Outward from the center: Bessel’s equation. What remains for R is 
r^2R'' + rR' + (k^2r^2 - m^2)R = 0,
 Bessel’s equation. It depends on r only through kr, so its solutions are functions of kr. Of its two essentially different solutions, one, the Bessel function J_m(kr), is finite at the center; the other becomes infinite there, which would take infinite energy, so it is not a free mode. J_m plays the part the sine played on a string: it wiggles like a cosine or sine whose swings slowly shrink.

5. The rim picks out the frequencies. The rim condition R(a) = 0 says J_m(ka) = 0: ka must be a zero of J_m. Writing j_{m,n} for the n-th positive zero, k = j_{m,n}/a. The zeros have no closed form and are computed numerically; those of J_0 are 2.405, 5.520, 8.654, …, in the ratios 1 : 2.30 : 3.60.

The round drum’s spectrum. Modes J_m(j_{m,n}\,r/a)\cos m\theta and J_m(j_{m,n}\,r/a)\sin m\theta, for m = 0, 1, 2, \dots and n = 1, 2, 3, \dots, with frequencies 
f_{m,n} = \frac{c\,j_{m,n}}{2\pi a}.
 In order, relative to the lowest: 1, 1.593, 2.136, 2.295, 2.653, 2.917, … Each frequency with m \ge 1 belongs to two modes, the cosine and the sine, the same pattern turned. The eigenvalues of A are \lambda_{m,n} = c^2 j_{m,n}^2/a^2.

These are all the modes: expanding any mode in a Fourier series in \theta (page 3) reduces -\Delta X = k^2X, term by term, to Bessel’s equation for each m.



DetailsWhy the pairs are exact, and how the zeros are spaced

Each frequency with m \ge 1 belongs to exactly two modes because Bessel functions of different whole-number orders never share a positive zero; this was conjectured by Bourget and proved by Carl Ludwig Siegel in 1929. This page computes the zeros numerically. For large n they approach j_{m,n} \approx (n + \tfrac m2 - \tfrac14)\pi: evenly spaced for one fixed m, but shifted by an amount that depends on m. The round head’s symmetry shows up as a multiplicity of 2.

title: Why does a drum thud?
text:
4 · On the spectrum diagram
These are the frequencies in your last strike, as multiples of the lowest: each stem is one j_{m,n}/j_{0,1} from the result box of stage 3. After 1×, the next few, 1.59×, 2.14× and 2.30×, sit between the lines. Higher up the stems crowd together, so some land near a line by chance, such as 2.92× and 4.06×; but no base frequency in the range we hear as pitch puts them all on or near lines. Each stem’s height is how strongly that mode sounds at the listening ring for the strike you made: strike somewhere else and the heights change, never the positions. Tap a stem to see that mode on the drumhead and hear it alone.
