title: Why does a drum thud?
text:
5 · What we hear
Off the lines and fading fast: a thud. The frequencies of stage 3 don’t sit at whole-number multiples of any base frequency we hear as pitch, so the sound doesn’t repeat at any such rate; and a real head gives its energy to the air quickly, so it fades fast. Together, a thud.
A struck head moves as the sum of its modes, u = \sum a_{m,n} X_{m,n} e^{-t/\tau_{m,n}} \cos(2\pi f_{m,n} t + \phi_{m,n}), each with its own fading time \tau_{m,n} (damping, added to the model), so its sound is a sum of tones at the frequencies of stage 3; the drum demo at the top synthesizes it exactly this way.
Why the frequencies miss the lines. The frequencies are the zeros of the Bessel functions, scaled. For the modes with no spokes, the zeros of J_0 come at nearly even steps, about \pi apart, but the first one is short, about 0.77\pi rather than \pi, so the later zeros are not multiples of the first: the frequencies go 1 : 2.30 : 3.60. Each number of spokes gives its own sequence, shifted by a different amount, and the sequences interleave at unrelated places. Merged, they give the drum’s list 1×, 1.59×, 2.14×, 2.30×, 2.65×, 2.92×, …, scattered between the lines. One more pattern: every mode with spokes comes in a pair, the same pattern turned, with exactly the same frequency. That is the round drum’s symmetry, heard in its spectrum.
The sand draws the still lines. In 1808 Ernst Chladni showed the French Institute in Paris, the body that then held the Academy of Sciences, a trick: sprinkle sand on a metal plate, draw a violin bow along its edge, and the sand leaps into a pattern, a different one for each note. The sand is jostled wherever the plate moves and comes to rest where it doesn’t, so each pattern is one mode’s still lines. Here is the same trick on a drumhead: pick a frequency and watch where the sand goes.


  
  
  Sprinkle fresh sandHear this note
  
  Each button drives the drumhead at one of its own frequencies, given as a multiple of the lowest. Every grain is jostled in proportion to how much the head moves under it, so grains drift until they reach a place where the head stays still. Chladni used stiff metal plates, whose operator involves bending, not tension; the sand behaves the same way on both.


Napoleon offered a prize for explaining the patterns. Sophie Germain won it in 1816, the first woman to receive the Paris Academy’s grand prize in mathematics, with a theory that was still incomplete; Gustav Kirchhoff gave the full theory of vibrating plates, with the correct edge conditions, in 1850. Finding the still lines and finding the frequencies are one problem: on a drumhead, the one on this page; on a plate, the same problem with the plate’s own operator.



PreciselyWhere the sand collects uses polar coordinates

The mode J_m(kr)\cos m\theta with k = j_{m,n}/a is zero where \cos m\theta = 0, at 2m angles, which pair up into m lines through the center, and along the circles where J_m(kr) = 0 inside the rim, n - 1 of them for the n-th zero. Those are exactly the lines where the sand collects.


Where you strike. A sharp strike starts each mode in proportion to how far that mode moves at the point struck. Every mode with spokes stays still at the center, so a strike at dead center sounds only the round modes, those with no spokes; a strike on one of a mode’s still lines leaves that mode silent. The two drums below use this.



DetailsHow strongly a strike excites each mode, in this model uses integrals over an area

Number the modes X_1, X_2, \dots in order of frequency. A sharp strike, a brief push at a point p, gives mode i a starting speed in proportion to X_i(p), the mode’s height at the point struck, the same rule as the piano’s hammer on page 7. We model what you hear as the speed of the head at a listening point q, which picks up mode i in proportion to X_i(q). Dividing by \iint X_i^2\,dA, the integral of the mode’s square over the head, removes the arbitrary size of each shape. So mode i sounds with weight X_i(p)\,X_i(q)\big/\iint X_i^2\,dA. (A real drum radiates sound from its whole head, and some modes radiate better than others; this model ignores that.)


One drumhead, two drums. A bass drum and a kettledrum, one of the timpani, both start from this operator, yet one booms and the other plays a note. Three things separate them, where the head is struck, what surrounds it, and which modes fade first; step through them below. On the kettledrum, the air the head must push pulls the spoke modes, those with one or more lines through the center and no still circle inside the rim, close to 2, 3, 4 and 5 times a common base (HyperPhysics; Fletcher and Rossing), and the strike point and the fast fading of the round modes leave mostly those. Players and acousticians name the note at the lowest of them, the (1,1) mode, the drum’s “principal tone” (Vienna’s Institute of Musical Acoustics); the next sit a fifth, an octave and a major tenth (an octave plus a major third, ratio 5 : 2) above it. That is not quite what page 0’s rule predicts: frequencies near 2, 3, 4 and 5 times a base nearly repeat at the base’s rate, an octave below the (1,1), and HyperPhysics notes that the missing-fundamental effect might then give the drum that lower pitch. Which octave the ear names when a sound fits two pitches an octave apart is a question about hearing rather than about the drumhead, and this series doesn’t settle it.

A toy model; the fold below gives its numbers and what it misses.





DetailsThe toy model, the kettle, and other drums uses integrals over an area

Where each drum is struck. A concert bass drum is played slightly off center; center playing, punchier and with less sustain, is kept for rhythmic passages (Graham 2017; Aleo, Interlochen 2023). There the spoke modes move little, so among the lowest modes the round ones dominate. Players muffle the head with a leg or a towel when the music calls for short notes, and let it ring for long ones (Aleo, Interlochen 2023); the step-through’s Muffle button does the first. Timpanists strike between halfway and three-quarters of the way out (HyperPhysics), roughly a third of the way in from the rim (Graham 2017). With the weight |X(p)|\big/\big(\iint X^2\,dA\big)^{1/2} for a strike at p, on a head of radius 1, the lowest round mode (0,1) has 1.09 at the center, 0.73 at halfway and 0.37 at three-quarters, while the spoke modes (1,1) to (4,1) have between 0.74 and 1.19 anywhere from halfway to three-quarters: lower than the spoke modes’ across the whole range. Nearer halfway the stick also sits close to the inner still circles of the modes (0,2), (1,2), (2,2) and (3,2), which lie between 0.44 and 0.65 of the radius, which quiets those too. The clear note also relies on the remaining modes being weaker or fading faster, which this page takes from measurements (Fletcher and Rossing, chapter 18) rather than deriving.
The air’s mass. Treat the air on both sides of the head as not squeezable, and each mode, locally, as a ripple of wavenumber k = j_{m,n}/a, whose crests are about \pi/k apart. The air such a ripple sets moving reaches about 1/k from the head on each side, which adds a mass of about 2\rho/k per unit area (\rho \approx 1.2 kg/m³ for air) to the head’s own \sigma: 
\omega^2 = \frac{T k^2}{\sigma + 2\rho/k}, \qquad f \propto \frac{k}{\sqrt{\sigma + 2\rho/k}} ,
 so coarse shapes, with small k, slow down most. This is the hub’s added mass: it can only lower frequencies. A typical Mylar kettledrum head has \sigma \approx 0.26 kg/m², on drums of radius 0.32 to 0.355 m (Packer 1993); with a = 0.33 m, 2\rho a/\sigma \approx 3.0. The spoke modes (1,1) to (4,1) move from 1 : 1.34 : 1.67 : 1.98 to 1 : 1.42 : 1.83 : 2.24, halfway to 1.5 : 2 : 2.5. The rest of the shift comes from a full calculation of the air inside and around a finite head (Christian, Davis, Tubis, Anderson, Mills and Rossing 1984), not from the kettle’s air spring, its uniform pressure.
The kettle. The nearly sealed kettle (it has a small vent) acts as a spring on the volume the head sweeps, V = \iint u\,dA, adding \tfrac12\eta V^2 to the stored energy for some constant \eta > 0. The operator gains the term (\eta/\sigma)\,\mathbf 1\langle\mathbf 1, \cdot\rangle, where \mathbf 1 is the constant shape and \sigma the head’s mass per unit area: a term of rank one. Every mode with m \ge 1 has \iint X\,dA = 0, because \int_0^{2\pi}\cos m\theta\,d\theta = 0, so \big(A + (\eta/\sigma)\,\mathbf 1\langle\mathbf 1, \cdot\rangle\big)X = AX, and in this model it keeps its frequency exactly. Only the round modes are raised, and since the new term couples them to each other, their shapes change too; the explorable treats each on its own. The hub’s principle says the same in general: added stiffness never lowers a frequency.
The bass drum’s second head. A bass drum has a head on each end of its shell, coupled through the air inside, which splits its two lowest modes, (0,1) and (1,1); the two heads’ lowest modes are commonly tuned about a fourth apart (HyperPhysics). Not modelled here.
Other drums. Toms are tuned to rough pitches, and a snare drum’s crack comes from the wires, the snares, stretched across its lower head. The tabla and the mridangam reach near-whole-number overtones a different way: a patch of paste loads the center of the head, which makes the head’s density non-uniform, outside this page’s model (Raman and Kumar 1920; Raman 1934).

title: Why does a drum thud?
text:
What we found
An ideal uniform drumhead, A = -c^2\Delta with the rim held still, has its frequencies at the zeros of Bessel functions, 1×, 1.59×, 2.14×, 2.30×, … the lowest: off the lines of the spectrum diagram, so a plain drum thuds. A kettledrum is the same head in different surroundings: the air it pushes pulls its spoke modes near 2 : 3 : 4 : 5, the strike point and the fast-fading round modes leave mostly those, and you hear a note. The next page turns the question around.

One operator family, as a first model. Toms, snares, bass drums and timpani share this operator on a disk. They differ in tension, size and the mass of the head, and in what surrounds it, and the air in and around a drum changes the operator a little, or, for the timpani, enough to matter.

← 6b Harmonica · The Shape of a Sound · Spectrum of an operator · Map · 8 Drum →
Listen first: an octave tuned to exactly 2 : 1, then a stretched one. The slow wobble in loudness is called a beat.

title: Why do piano tuners stretch octaves?
section: 1 · Newton’s law: the equation of motion
text:
1 · Newton’s law: the equation of motion
Mathematics used: partial derivatives (explained) and the small-angle approximation.
Here is where the piano’s frequencies come from. Apply Newton’s law, mass times acceleration equals force, to one short piece of wire. Two forces act on it, tension and bending, and the piano’s whole story is that they add.
1. One small piece. Follow the stretch of wire between x and x+dx, and let u(x,t) be its height above the rest line at time t; subscripts are partial derivatives. The piece has mass \mu\,dx, where \mu is the mass per unit length, and vertical acceleration u_{tt}, so Newton’s law for its up-and-down motion reads 
\mu\,dx\,u_{tt} = \text{net force on the piece}.

2. Tension pulls a curved piece toward the inside of its curve. The rest of the wire pulls on each end of the piece with the tension T, along the wire.

  
  
  
  
  
  TT
  xx+dx
  T uₓ(x)curved piece, mass μ dx
  T uₓ(x+dx)

At the right end the pull points along the wire, which makes a small angle \theta with the horizontal there. Its upward part is T\sin\theta; for a small angle \sin\theta \approx \tan\theta (both are about \theta in radians), and \tan\theta is the slope u_x(x+dx), so the upward part is T\,u_x(x+dx). At the left end it is -T\,u_x(x). Together, 
T\,\big[u_x(x+dx) - u_x(x)\big] \approx T\,u_{xx}\,dx .
 A straight piece feels no net pull; a curved one is pulled toward the inside of its curve. This is the violin string’s force, unchanged.
3. Bending pushes back too. Steel also resists being bent, exactly like the kalimba’s tine, and the kalimba page derives this force step by step. How sharply the wire bends, its curvature u_{xx}, sets a turning effect inside it, the bending moment EI\,u_{xx}. How that moment changes along the wire sets the sideways force across each cut, the shear force -EI\,u_{xxx}. And how the shear force changes along the wire is the net force on the piece: 
\text{bending force} = -EI\,u_{xxxx}\,dx ,
 where E is steel’s Young’s modulus, how stiff the material is, and I = \pi d^4/64 is the second moment of area of a round wire of diameter d, how strongly its cross-section resists bending.
4. Newton’s law. The two forces simply add: 
\mu\,dx\,u_{tt} = T\,u_{xx}\,dx - EI\,u_{xxxx}\,dx .
 Dividing by \mu\,dx, and writing c^2 = T/\mu and \kappa^2 = EI/\mu, 
u_{tt} = c^2\,u_{xx} - \kappa^2\,u_{xxxx}.

What we assumed. A plain (unwound) steel wire: bass strings are wound with copper, which adds mass but little stiffness. Small slopes; a tension that does not change as the wire flexes; a uniform wire; the spin of each thin slice neglected (Rayleigh’s correction for it adds a small term); and no damping, which the fold in stage 5 adds back.

title: Why do piano tuners stretch octaves?
text:
2 · The operator
Dividing by the mass per unit length puts the equation in the series’ form u_{tt} = -A\,u: the force per unit mass is a fixed rule applied to the wire’s shape, and that rule is the wire’s operator. The ends complete it. The bridge at one end and a metal bearing point at the other hold the wire in place, so u = 0 there. If they let the wire pivot freely they exert no bending moment, and the moment is EI\,u_{xx}, so also u_{xx} = 0. These are called pinned ends. Real piano strings are held a little more firmly than pinned, which shifts the numbers slightly but not the picture.

The piano wire’s operator. The equation of motion is u_{tt} = -A\,u, with 
A = -c^2\frac{d^2}{dx^2} + \kappa^2\frac{d^4}{dx^4},
 where c^2 = T/\mu and \kappa^2 = EI/\mu, acting on shapes with u = u_{xx} = 0 at both ends. The first term is the string’s operator, from tension; the second is the kalimba’s, from bending. A piano wire is both at once: operators add. In words: the force per unit mass on each point is the string’s pull toward the inside of the curve plus the bar’s push back against bending.

title: Why do piano tuners stretch octaves?
text:
3 · Its spectrum
A mode is a shape X that the operator only rescales: A X = \lambda X, with the number \lambda called its eigenvalue. Released in that shape, the wire keeps it and swings as X(x)\cos\omega t, with \omega = \sqrt{\lambda}, so at the frequency f = \sqrt{\lambda}/2\pi. The list of all the eigenvalues is the operator’s spectrum. Here is the wire’s.
1. Try a sine, which already satisfies the pinned ends. Take X = \sin(kx) with k = n\pi/L, where L is the wire’s length and n = 1, 2, 3, \dots It is zero at both ends, and so is X'' = -k^2X: both pinned conditions hold.
2. Apply the operator: each term rescales the same sine. Two derivatives give X'' = -k^2X and four give X'''' = k^4X, so 
A X = \big(c^2k^2 + \kappa^2k^4\big)\,X .
 The sine is rescaled, not reshaped: it is an eigenfunction, with eigenvalue \lambda_n = c^2k^2 + \kappa^2k^4. Each term rescales the same sine, so the string’s eigenvalue and the bar’s simply add. That is special to pinned ends, where the two operators share their eigenfunctions; with clamped ends the formula needs a small correction. There are no other modes: the sines already form a complete set (page 4), and since the operator is symmetric, an eigenfunction for any other eigenvalue would be perpendicular to every sine, hence zero.
3. The frequencies: the string’s, nudged up by stiffness. Factoring out the string’s part, 
\omega_n^2 = \lambda_n = c^2k^2\Big(1 + \frac{EI}{T}\,k^2\Big),
 and with k = n\pi/L, 
\omega_n^2 = \Big(\frac{n\pi c}{L}\Big)^2\Big(1 + \frac{\pi^2EI}{TL^2}\,n^2\Big).
 Taking the square root and dividing by 2\pi gives the result.

The piano wire’s spectrum. Modes \sin(n\pi x/L), n = 1, 2, 3, \dots, with frequencies 
f_n = n f_0\sqrt{1 + Bn^2},
 with eigenvalues \lambda_n = (2\pi f_n)^2 and the stiffness constant B = \pi^2 EI/(T L^2). Here f_0 = c/2L is the lowest frequency the same wire would have without stiffness; the actual fundamental is f_1 = f_0\sqrt{1 + B}. Each partial sits at f_n/f_1 = n\sqrt{(1 + Bn^2)/(1 + B)} times the fundamental: a little above n, more so the larger n.

The stiffness constant B is small, but it multiplies n^2, so the fundamental barely moves while high partials run noticeably sharp: the string is slightly inharmonic.
How big is B? For a middle C wire, roughly d = 1 mm and L = 0.6 m, with steel’s E = 2\times10^{11} Pa and density 7850 kg/m³; a tension of about 610 N then gives middle C. So I \approx 4.9\times10^{-14} m^4 and B \approx 4.4\times10^{-4}. The 10th partial (the fundamental counts as the 1st), at 10f_0\sqrt{1 + 100B}, then sits 1200\log_2\sqrt{(1 + 100B)/(1 + B)} \approx 37 cents sharp of ten times the fundamental, about a third of a semitone. These numbers are rough; real strings vary. Since I grows like the fourth power of the diameter and B falls like 1/L^2, short treble strings, thick for their length, are the stiffest.

title: Why do piano tuners stretch octaves?
text:
4 · On the spectrum diagram
Here are the frequencies of a piano note, middle C, or the last key you played on the keyboard below. Each stem is one f_n/f_1 = n\sqrt{(1 + Bn^2)/(1 + B)} from the result box of stage 3, with that key’s B. They sit a little sharp of the gray lines, and the higher the partial, the further sharp; the readout gives the shift in cents, hundredths of a semitone. The low partials are so close to the lines that the ear still hears one clear note. Each stem’s height is how strongly the hammer starts that mode; the hammer strikes an eighth of the way along, where the 8th and 16th modes stand still, so those two are nearly silent.

title: Why do piano tuners stretch octaves?
text:
5 · What we hear
Why exact octaves beat. A tuner sets an octave by ear, listening for beats between the lower note’s second partial and the upper note’s fundamental. Two nearly equal frequencies played together beat at a rate equal to their difference. The spectrum says where the lower note’s second partial sits: 
\frac{f_2}{f_1} = 2\sqrt{\frac{1 + 4B}{1 + B}} \approx 2\Big(1 + \frac{3B}{2}\Big),
 using \sqrt{1+x} \approx 1 + x/2 (square it: (1 + x/2)^2 = 1 + x + x^2/4, and x^2/4 is tiny) and 1/\sqrt{1+x} \approx 1 - x/2 for small x. So the second partial is more than twice the fundamental, by a factor of about 1 + 3B/2. An upper note tuned to exactly twice the fundamental sits just below it, and the two beat. Raising the upper note slows this beat and makes the octave slightly wider than 2 : 1. Tuners also listen to other pairs, such as the lower note’s fourth partial against the upper note’s second, and the upper note’s own partials run sharp too, so stiffness makes it impossible to silence all of the beats at once. So the tuner can only reduce the beating: real tuning is a compromise. Tick “Play every partial” in the demo at the top to hear it: the stretched octave then wobbles too. On a stiff string, “exactly 2 : 1” lines up the wrong pair of frequencies.
The stretch is largest at the ends of the keyboard. Repeated octave by octave across the keyboard, this is stretch tuning: compared with equal temperament, the top of a piano ends up sharp and the bottom flat. Two things make the stretch grow toward the ends. The small widenings add up, octave by octave, away from the middle; and the most inharmonic strings are at the two ends: the short treble strings, and the bass strings, which the size of the piano keeps short for their pitch. O. L. Railsback measured this stretch on pianos tuned by ear in the 1930s; the plot of how far each note sits from equal temperament is called the Railsback curve: close to equal temperament in the middle of the keyboard, flat in the bass, sharp in the treble.
A struck wire moves as the sum of its modes, u = \sum_n a_n X_n \cos(2\pi f_n t + \phi_n), so its sound is a sum of tones at the frequencies f_n of stage 3, each fading at its own rate (damping, added to the model); the demos on this page synthesize it exactly this way. Because the low partials sit so close to the lines, the ear hears one clear note.
Hammer, dampers and pedals: none of them moves a frequency. The frequencies belong to the operator, set by the wire’s tension and stiffness. The hammer decides how much of each mode starts, and the felt dampers decide how fast each mode dies. Every control a pianist touches does one of these two things; only the tuner’s wrench, which changes the tension, changes the operator and moves the frequencies. You can try them all on the whole piano further down.



DetailsWhat each control changes

The hammer starts each mode in proportion to the mode’s own height where the hammer hits, so a mode that stands still there stays silent. In a simple model, the felt dampers make each mode die at a rate proportional to how much it moves under the felt. The pedals act on one or the other:

Step-by-step derivationThe full string equation, the hammer weights and the damping rates uses integrals of products of modes and a first-order approximation

The operator is only part of the string’s equation. A real string is also pushed by the hammer and loses energy to damping; here f(x,t) is a force, not a frequency: 
\mu\,u_{tt} + b(x,t)\,u_t = T\,u_{xx} - EI\,u_{xxxx} + f(x,t).

Each term has one job. The operator’s term, T\,u_{xx} - EI\,u_{xxxx} (that is, -\mu A u), fixes the frequencies and the mode shapes. The forcing f is the hammer, and it fixes how much of each mode is excited. The damping b is the felt dampers plus small internal losses, and it fixes how fast each mode dies. Every control a pianist touches acts on f or on b. Only the tuner’s wrench, which changes T, touches the operator.
Both effects are read off the mode shapes X_n(x) = \sin(n\pi x/L). A hammer blow at x_h gives mode n a weight proportional to X_n(x_h), the mode’s own height at the hammer. The drum on the next page uses the same rule. A damper felt resting on a short stretch W of the string makes mode n’s swing shrink like e^{-\gamma_n t}, and for weak damping (to first order in b, that is, ignoring terms in b^2) the decay rate is 
\gamma_n = \frac{\int_W b\,X_n^2\,dx}{2\mu\int_0^L X_n^2\,dx}.
 A mode is damped in proportion to how much it moves under the felt, and its frequency shifts only by an amount proportional to \gamma_n^2, negligible for weak damping. A mode with a node under the felt barely notices the damper: in the view of the inside of the piano further down, slide the damper to L/8, where the hammer also sits, and the 8th mode, which has a still point there, is not excited and barely damped.
In the table above, the dampers and the sustain pedal change b; the soft pedal and the practice mute change f; only the tuning pin changes the operator.
1. Expand in modes. Write u(x,t) = \sum_n q_n(t)\,X_n(x), with A X_n = \omega_n^2X_n and the pinned conditions.
2. Project. Substitute into the full equation, multiply by X_m and integrate along the string. The operator is symmetric with these boundary conditions (in fact self-adjoint), by integrating by parts as on the circle page, so the X_n are orthogonal: \int_0^L X_mX_n\,dx = 0 for m \ne n. The acceleration and operator terms collapse to one term each: 
\mu N_m\,(\ddot q_m + \omega_m^2 q_m) + \sum_n D_{mn}\,\dot q_n = F_m(t),
 with N_m = \int X_m^2\,dx, D_{mn} = \int b\,X_mX_n\,dx and F_m = \int f\,X_m\,dx.
3. The hammer. The felt touches a short stretch near x_h, so F_m(t) \approx X_m(x_h)\,P(t), where P(t) is the total force. Every mode gets the same push in time, weighted by X_m(x_h): the mode’s own height at the hammer.
4. The damper. If the damping is weak, the cross terms D_{mn} with m \ne n change the answer only at second order. Keeping the diagonal leaves a damped oscillator for each mode, 
\ddot q_m + 2\gamma_m\,\dot q_m + \omega_m^2 q_m = 0, \qquad \gamma_m = \frac{D_{mm}}{2\mu N_m},
 whose solution e^{-\gamma_m t}\cos\big(\sqrt{\omega_m^2 - \gamma_m^2}\,t\big) decays at the rate \gamma_m while its frequency moves only by order \gamma_m^2/\omega_m.
5. Honest limits. A real damper is not weak: it stops a note in a fraction of a second. The formula gives the right picture, that modes are damped by how much they move under the felt, but not exact decay times.

title: Why do piano tuners stretch octaves?
text:
What we found
A piano wire is a string and a bar at once, A = -c^2\,d^2/dx^2 + \kappa^2\,d^4/dx^4, and with pinned ends its spectrum, f_n = n f_0\sqrt{1 + Bn^2}, puts each partial slightly above its whole-number multiple, more so the higher it goes. So an exact 2 : 1 octave beats, and tuners stretch octaves to reduce the beating, most at the ends of the keyboard; the hammer, the dampers and the pedals change how the modes start and die, not where they sit. The next page turns the line into a sheet: the drum.

The stiff string’s operator family. Every real string is a little stiff, so a more exact model puts guitar and harp strings in this operator family too, with a smaller stiffness constant B. The piano is where stiffness is large enough to hear, and large enough to change how pianos are tuned.

DetailsGrand pianos: the middle pedal and the two-stage decay

On a grand piano the middle pedal is usually the sostenuto, which holds up only the dampers of keys already down. Most notes have two or three strings, and Weinreich showed that their coupling through the bridge, each string’s motion slightly shaking the others, produces the piano’s two-stage decay: a loud start that fades fast, then a quiet, long aftersound. A grand’s soft pedal strikes fewer of the strings, so the coupled motion starts differently. This model leaves the coupling out.

DetailsWhere the dampers sit: under-damper and birdcage uprights

Where the dampers touch the string matters, because each mode is damped in proportion to its motion under the felt. Close to an end every low mode barely moves, so a damper there hardly damps the bass. In most modern uprights the dampers sit below the hammers, nearer the middle of the string; in older “birdcage” uprights they sat above the hammers, near the end. Piano restorers report that the under-damper design stops the strings better, partly because its dampers are closer to the middle of the string (Sykes). The slider in the view above moves the damper and shows the effect on each mode.





Reader questionWhat does a damper do, and what would a piano without dampers sound like?

Without dampers, releasing a key would do nothing: every string would ring until it died on its own, exactly as if the sustain pedal were always down. On a real piano each key lifts a felt damper off its strings; letting go drops the damper back and stops the note within a fraction of a second. The sustain pedal lifts all the dampers at once, so released notes keep ringing. The keyboard above models both. The top 20 keys have no dampers at all, as on a real piano: those short strings die out quickly by themselves.

title: Why does a light touch make a string jump an octave?
section: 1 · Newton’s law: the equation of motion
text:
1 · Newton’s law: the equation of motion
Mathematics used: partial derivatives (explained) and the small-angle approximation.
Apply Newton’s law, mass times acceleration equals force, to one short piece of the string. The only force on the piece comes from the tension pulling at its two ends, and it turns out to depend only on how the string bends there.
1. Set up the string. Let the string run along x from the nut, at x = 0, to the bridge, at x = L. It is stretched with tension T, a pulling force, and has mass \mu per unit length. Write u(x, t) for its height above the straight line at position x and time t. Take the short piece between x and x + dx; its mass is \mu\,dx.
2. The tension pulls each end of the piece along the string. If the string at a point makes a small angle \theta with the straight line, the upward part of the pull is T\sin\theta; for a small angle \sin\theta \approx \tan\theta (both are about \theta in radians), and \tan\theta is the slope. So the upward part of the pull is the tension times the slope. At the right end the rest of the string pulls with upward part T\,u_x(x + dx); at the left end it pulls the other way, with upward part -T\,u_x(x). Here u_x is the slope, the derivative in x with the time held fixed (a partial derivative).

  
  
  
  
  
  TT
  xx + dx
  upward part of each pull ≈ T × slope

3. Add the two pulls. The net upward force on the piece is the difference of the slopes at its two ends, times T: 
T\,u_x(x + dx) - T\,u_x(x) \approx T\,u_{xx}\,dx ,
 where u_{xx}, the rate at which the slope changes, is the string’s curvature. On a hump the slope falls from left to right, u_{xx} < 0, and the net force pulls the piece down.
4. Newton’s law. The piece’s acceleration is u_{tt}, the second derivative of the height in time with x held fixed. Mass times acceleration equals force: \mu\,dx\;u_{tt} = T\,u_{xx}\,dx. Divide by \mu\,dx: 
u_{tt} = c^2\,u_{xx}, \qquad c^2 = \frac{T}{\mu}.
 This is the wave equation; c is the speed at which a bump runs along the string.
What we assumed. Small slopes, so that the tension stays T and its upward part is T times the slope; the same tension and mass per length everywhere; a perfectly flexible string, with no stiffness (a real string is slightly stiff: page 7); no air and no friction; and ends that are held perfectly still.



Step-by-step derivationThe same equation from beads with the ends tied uses matrices, as on page 2

Put N beads of mass m, spaced h apart, on a thread of tension T, with both ends tied, so u_0 = u_{N+1} = 0. The force on bead j is the one derived on the ring page, so m\ddot u_j = \frac{T}{h}(u_{j+1} - 2u_j + u_{j-1}). The matrix is now the ring’s matrix without its two corner entries: 
K = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 & & \\ -1 & 2 & \ddots & \\ & \ddots & \ddots & -1\\ & & -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}.
 Its eigenvectors are v_j = \sin\big(n\pi j/(N+1)\big), the sampled sines, with eigenvalues 4\sin^2\big(n\pi/(2(N+1))\big) for n = 1, \dots, N. To check: \sin(\alpha(j+1)) + \sin(\alpha(j-1)) = 2\cos\alpha\,\sin(\alpha j), so (Kv)_j = (2 - 2\cos\alpha)\,v_j = 4\sin^2(\alpha/2)\,v_j with \alpha = n\pi/(N+1), and the tied ends hold because \sin 0 = \sin n\pi = 0. As on the ring, letting N \to \infty with L = (N+1)h and \mu = m/h fixed gives the wave equation and the frequencies f_n = \frac{n}{2L}\sqrt{T/\mu} found below.

title: Why does a light touch make a string jump an octave?
text:
2 · The operator
Read the equation of motion as a rule. The acceleration of each point is c^2u_{xx}: take the string’s shape, find its curvature at every point, and multiply by c^2. Minus that, the restoring force per unit mass, is the string’s operator, A = -c^2\,d^2/dx^2, and the equation reads u_{tt} = -Au.
The ends are tied. At the nut and the bridge the string cannot move: u(0, t) = 0 and u(L, t) = 0 at every moment. So A only ever acts on shapes that stay still at both ends. This restriction is a boundary condition, here a Dirichlet condition. An operator is the rule together with the shapes it is allowed to act on, so the tied ends are part of the operator: they decide which shapes are eigenfunctions, and so which frequencies the string has.

The string’s operator. The equation of motion is 
\begin{gathered} u_{tt} = -A\,u, \\ A = -c^2\,\frac{d^2}{dx^2}, \qquad c^2 = \frac{T}{\mu}, \end{gathered}
 acting on shapes X on [0, L] with X(0) = X(L) = 0. In words: A takes a shape and returns minus c^2 times its curvature, and only shapes that stay still at both ends are allowed.

title: Why does a light touch make a string jump an octave?
text:
3 · Its spectrum
A mode is a shape that the operator only rescales: AX = \lambda X. The shape X is an eigenfunction, and the number \lambda its eigenvalue. Released in that shape, the string keeps it and swings at the angular frequency \omega = \sqrt\lambda, that is, at f = \sqrt\lambda/2\pi in hertz. The list of all eigenvalues is the spectrum. Here is the whole computation.
1. Which shapes does the operator only rescale? AX = \lambda X says -c^2X'' = \lambda X. Write \lambda = c^2k^2 with k > 0; then X'' = -k^2X, a shape whose curvature is minus k^2 times itself. Its solutions are the waves X = a\cos kx + b\sin kx. (Zero and negative \lambda give no shape that stays still at both ends; see the first proof fold below.)
2. Hold the nut still. X(0) = 0 forces a = 0, so X = b\sin kx.
3. Hold the bridge still. X(L) = 0 then needs \sin kL = 0, so kL is a whole multiple of \pi: k = n\pi/L for n = 1, 2, 3, \dots The shape \sin(n\pi x/L) has n arches.
4. Turn the eigenvalues into frequencies. The eigenvalues are \lambda_n = c^2k_n^2 = (n\pi c/L)^2, so 
f_n = \frac{\sqrt{\lambda_n}}{2\pi} = \frac{n\,c}{2L} = \frac{n}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}} = n\,f_1 .


The string’s spectrum. Eigenfunctions: \sin(n\pi x/L), the shapes with n = 1, 2, 3, \dots arches. Eigenvalues: \lambda_n = (n\pi c/L)^2. Frequencies: f_n = n f_1, with 
f_1 = \frac{1}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}},
 exactly 1, 2, 3, … times the lowest. The lowest rises with the tension and falls with the length and the mass per length.

In plain words: a shape with n arches is n times shorter than the one-arch shape; a shorter shape bends more sharply, and the string pulls back in proportion to how sharply it bends, so it is pulled back n² times harder and swings n times faster. Each arch shape is exactly half of a wave on a loop twice as long, so the string keeps half of the loop’s waves from page 3. One thing does change: on a loop each frequency had two waves, one shifted along the loop; on a string a wave cannot run around, it reflects at the ends, and each frequency has a single shape, a standing wave.



ProofNo other eigenvalues uses integration by parts

Write the eigenvalue as \lambda = c^2 k^2 for some number k^2, so that -X'' = k^2 X. Multiply by X and integrate from 0 to L. Integrating by parts, the boundary term -X X' vanishes at both ends because X = 0 there: 
k^2\int_0^L X^2\,dx = \int_0^L (X')^2\,dx .
 So a zero or negative \lambda would need \int (X')^2\,dx \le 0, which only the constant shapes satisfy, and the only constant that vanishes at the ends is X = 0. Each eigenvalue (n\pi c/L)^2 has multiplicity 1: the boundary condition at the nut removed the cosine.





ProofThe string is half of a circle: the sine series as a Fourier series uses Fourier series and the uniqueness of solutions of the wave equation

Take a shape u on [0, L] with u(0) = u(L) = 0. Extend it to [-L, 0] by u(-x) = -u(x), an odd reflection, and then repeat with period 2L. The result is a shape on a loop of circumference 2L.

  
  
  
  
  0L−L
  stringodd reflection


Odd shapes stay odd. If u(x, t) solves the wave equation on the loop, so does -u(-x, t), since two derivatives in x do not change sign under x \mapsto -x. Starting from an odd shape at rest, both are the same solution by uniqueness, so the motion stays odd.
Odd shapes on the loop are exactly string shapes. An odd periodic shape vanishes at 0, because u(0) = -u(0), and at L, because u(L) = u(-L) = -u(L). Conversely every string shape extends this way.
So the string’s eigenfunctions are the loop’s odd eigenfunctions. On a loop of circumference 2L the eigenfunctions of -c^2\,d^2/dx^2 are \cos(n\pi x/L) and \sin(n\pi x/L), with eigenvalues (n\pi c/L)^2. The odd ones are the sines. Each eigenvalue keeps one of its two eigenfunctions, which is why the multiplicity drops from 2 to 1.

The sine series of a string shape, u = \sum_n b_n\sin(n\pi x/L), is therefore the Fourier series of its odd extension, and everything proved on the circle page carries over: every string shape is a sum of the string’s modes. The same trick with an even reflection, u(-x) = u(x), gives the cosines and the condition u'(0) = u'(L) = 0; the next page combines both reflections for air in a tube.

Below, each stem’s height is how far that mode swings just after the pluck; under the demo at the top, how far it still swings a quarter of a second later; the pluck decides how strongly each mode starts, and the finger decides how fast each one dies (stage 5). Touch at the middle and the odd stems die almost at once; what is left sits on every second line, the lines of a note twice as high. Touch at a third and only every third stem survives. Move the pluck point too: near the bridge the stems shrink slowly as they go up, and at the middle they shrink fast, with every second stem missing even without a finger.

title: Why does a light touch make a string jump an octave?
text:
5 · What we hear
A light touch keeps only the shapes that are still under the finger. The finger is a damper: a soft, lossy contact that takes energy from whatever moves under it. It does not hold the string still there, as a new end would (pressing down does that; see below). Where a shape has a still point, a node, the finger has nothing to grab, and that shape rings on. Every other shape moves under the finger and loses its energy to it within a moment. The shape \sin(n\pi x/L) is still at the middle exactly when n is even: 2, 4, 6, … arches, at 2, 4, 6, … times the open string’s frequency. The survivors repeat twice as often, so you hear a note an octave up. At a third, the survivors have 3, 6, 9, … arches: three times the frequency, an octave and a fifth up (a factor 2 times a factor 3/2). (In this simple model the finger drains each shape in proportion to how much that shape moves under it, the rule the piano page derives for felt dampers.)



PreciselyWhich modes survive a light touch uses the sine function

Let the finger touch the string at the distance s from the nut, and write X_n(x) = \sin(n\pi x/L) for the shape of mode n. In the model, the finger drains mode n at a rate proportional to X_n(s)^2, how much that mode moves under it. The modes that survive are the ones with a node right under the finger: \sin(n\pi s/L) = 0, which means ns/L is a whole number. At s = L/2 these are the even n, at 2f_1, 4f_1, 6f_1, \dots: a note with fundamental 2f_1. At s = L/3 they are n = 3, 6, 9, \dots, with fundamental 3f_1: an octave (a factor 2) and a fifth (a factor 3/2) up, since 2 \times 3/2 = 3.


The string’s motion is the sum of its modes, each swinging at its own frequency and fading at its own rate: 
u(x, t) = \sum_{n} a_n\,e^{-t/\tau_n}\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}\,\cos(2\pi f_n t + \phi_n).
 The demo’s sound is made this way: it adds up these modes at f_n = n \times 196 Hz, each weighted by its push on the bridge, which is what reaches your ear (see “Where you pluck” below); the stems show how far each mode swings. Because every f_n is a whole multiple of f_1, apart from the slow fading the sum repeats every 1/f_1 seconds, and a sound that repeats is a note at that rate (page 0).
Where you pluck sets the brightness. A pluck starts each shape according to how much of it is in the plucked triangle. What reaches your ear is the string’s push on the bridge, and for the same height a shape with more arches has steeper ends, so it pushes harder. Pluck near the bridge, and the first several shapes push the bridge about equally hard (near the end, a shape with n arches starts about 1/n as large but is n times as steep, so the pushes come out about equal; fold below): the sound is bright. Pluck at the middle, and every shape with an even number of arches is missing, since those stand still exactly where you pulled; the rest push the bridge less and less, the more arches they have: a mellow, hollow sound.



Step-by-step derivationHow much of each shape a pluck starts uses integration by parts

Every shape of the string is a sum \sum_n b_n\sin(n\pi x/L) of its modes (second proof fold above), and b_n says how much of mode n the shape contains. A string pulled aside a distance d at a point x_p from one end, and let go, starts as a triangle. With x_p measured from the nut, where x = 0, its sine coefficients are 
b_n = \frac{2dL^2}{\pi^2 x_p(L - x_p)}\cdot\frac{\sin(n\pi x_p/L)}{n^2}.
 Measuring x_p from the bridge instead only flips the sign of every second b_n, since \sin(n\pi(L - x_p)/L) = \pm\sin(n\pi x_p/L), and signs do not change how loud a mode is; from here on x_p is the distance from the bridge. What reaches your ear is driven by the force on the bridge, which is proportional to the string’s slope there and so to n\,b_n for mode n. Near the bridge, x_p small, \sin(n\pi x_p/L) \approx n\pi x_p/L for the first several modes, so n b_n hardly falls off at all: the high modes are strong and the sound is bright. At the middle, \sin(n\pi/2) is zero for every even n, and the rest have n b_n falling like 1/n: a mellower, hollow sound.
Where the formula comes from. Take L = 1 and write q = x_p. The starting shape is u_0(x) = dx/q for 0 \le x \le q and u_0(x) = d(1 - x)/(1 - q) for q \le x \le 1. Its sine coefficients are b_n = 2\int_0^1 u_0(x)\sin(n\pi x)\,dx, by the perpendicularity of the sines, which the string inherits from the circle page. Integrate by parts twice on each straight piece. Since u_0 vanishes at both ends and u_0'' = 0 on each piece, the only term left comes from the jump in slope at the corner, from d/q just left of it to -d/(1-q) just right of it: b_n = \frac{2}{n^2\pi^2}\big(\tfrac{d}{q} + \tfrac{d}{1-q}\big)\sin(n\pi q) = \frac{2d\sin(n\pi q)}{n^2\pi^2 q(1-q)}. The 1/n^2 comes from that single corner.


Pressing down makes a new end. Pressing a finger firmly onto the fingerboard is different: it ties the string down there, and only the piece between the finger and the bridge sounds. By the formula for f_1, a shorter string sounds higher, in inverse proportion to its length: two-thirds of the length sounds a fifth up, half the length an octave up, and the semitone positions bunch closer together toward the bridge. Play a whole violin: press and hold a string to bow it, slide sideways to finger it, or switch to plucking.


  
  
    Bow (hold)Pizzicato, plucked (tap)
     Wooden body
    Press and hold a string. Slide left and right to finger it.
  
  
  Left edge: the nut; right edge: the bridge. Ticks: where the finger goes for each semitone (fold below). Stems: the partials you hear; switching the body off or on changes their heights, never their positions.





DetailsWhere the finger goes for each semitone uses powers

The nut is the end of the string near the tuning pegs, and an open string is one not pressed down by a finger. With the finger at distance s from the nut, the vibrating length shrinks to L - s, so the pitch rises by the factor L/(L - s). In equal temperament the twelve semitones of an octave are equal ratios of frequency, so each is 2^{1/12}, and k semitones are 2^{k/12}. Solving L/(L - s) = 2^{k/12} gives s_k = (1 - 2^{-k/12})L: the semitone positions bunch together toward the bridge. These are the ticks on the violin’s fingerboard above.


The bow locks the note. A bow grips the string, drags it along until the string’s pull tears it free, lets it slip back, and grips it again, once per period. By 1860 Hermann von Helmholtz had watched this through a vibration microscope: the string forms two straight pieces joined by one sharp corner, which races between the bridge and the finger. This is Helmholtz motion. It repeats exactly, so its partials sit exactly on the lines. (The demo’s bowed voice adds a gentle vibrato, as players do, which wobbles the lines slightly.) That matters because a real string is slightly stiff, and its own frequencies run a little sharp of the lines (page 7): plucked, each mode rings at its own slightly sharp frequency and fades; bowed, the stick and slip lock the whole motion into exact repetition. The locking comes from the bow’s friction, which is not linear; this page shows it but does not derive it.


    
    BowedPlucked at 1/4
    
    Slowed about 500 times. The faint lens-shaped outline is the path the corner traces. Stems: the partials of the push on the bridge.
  




Step-by-step derivationHelmholtz motion as a sum of modes uses the plucked-string formula above

A vibration microscope’s lens rides on a vibrating tuning fork, so that a bright speck on the string traces a pattern revealing its motion. Helmholtz reported what he saw in 1860 and in his 1863 book. The expansion of Helmholtz motion in the string’s eigenfunctions is, for some overall size a, 
u(x,t) = \sum_{n\ge1} \frac{a}{n^2}\,\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}\,\sin(2\pi n f_1 t).
 Where this comes from: at each moment the string is two straight pieces, like a plucked string, with the corner at some point x_c. Helmholtz showed that the corner’s height is proportional to x_c(L - x_c), so it traces two arcs of a parabola, the lens in the demo, and that the corner moves at the wave speed c = 2Lf_1. Put that height in place of d in the pluck formula above: the factor x_c(L - x_c) cancels and b_n \propto \sin(n\pi x_c/L)/n^2. With x_c = 2Lf_1t this is \sin(2\pi nf_1t)/n^2; on the way back the corner runs along the lower arc, and the same formula covers it: for x_c between L and 2L, \sin(n\pi x_c/L) describes a corner at 2L - x_c with negative height. The motion repeats exactly every 1/f_1 seconds, so its partials sit exactly on nf_1. The force on the bridge is proportional to the string’s slope there, and the slope of \sin(n\pi x/L) carries an extra factor n\pi/L, so partial n pushes the bridge with strength proportional to 1/n. On an ideal string a pluck also gives exact multiples of f_1; the difference between plucking and bowing shows only on a real, slightly stiff string, as described above.


The body changes loudness, not pitch. The string itself moves very little air. It rocks the bridge, the bridge shakes the wooden body, and the body moves the air. Each step is linear: shaken at one frequency, it responds at that same frequency, only louder or quieter and a little delayed. So the body can change each partial’s height but can never move it to another frequency. Toggle the wooden body on the violin above: the stems change height and stay where they are.

title: Why does a light touch make a string jump an octave?
text:
What we found
Tied at both ends, the string’s operator A = -c^2\,d^2/dx^2 has the arch shapes \sin(n\pi x/L) as its modes, at exactly n f_1 with f_1 = \frac{1}{2L}\sqrt{T/\mu}: the boundary condition is part of the operator and decides the frequencies. A light touch is a damper: it drains the modes that move under the finger and leaves the ones with a node there, at the middle the even ones, an octave up. The next page keeps the operator and changes the ends, for the air in a tube.

The string’s operator family. Guitar, cello and harp strings obey the same equation with the same tied ends, so the series puts them in one operator family with the violin string: the same operator up to its constants. They differ in length, tension and mass per length, which set the lowest frequency, and in how they are played: plucked (guitar, harp) or bowed (violin, cello).

How to Break Nested For Loop
text:
2 Double Nested for Loop
Here, the program halts right after (i,j) reaches (2,1), which is what we want.

for i in range(4): # Layer 1
    print(f"Layer 1 for i = {i}: start")
    for j in range(3): # Layer 2
        print(f"  {i} {j}")
        if (i, j) == (2, 1):
            break
    else: # reached <=> for loop layer 2 was broken
        print(f"  Layer 2 for i = {i}: finished")
        continue # continuing for the enclosing for loop (layer 1), thus ignoring the "break"
    break # reached <=> continue was not called <=> for loop layer 2 was broken

text:
1 Background

Proposition 1 For any random variable X, we have 
    X = F_X^{-1}(U).



Proof. For any x, we have 
    P(X \le x) = F_X(x) = P(U \le F_X(x)) = P(F_X^{-1}(U) \le x).
 Thus X = F_X^{-1}(U).

title: Inverse Sampling Transform
section: 2 Application: Uniform Sampling on a Disk
text:
2 Application: Uniform Sampling on a Disk
Now, we want to perform uniform sampling on the unit disk. We use polar coordinates; more specifically, we take r\cos(\theta), r\sin(\theta), where

r \in [0,1] such that P(r) \propto r (\Rightarrow P(r) = 2r)
\theta \sim U(0,2\pi)

The key lies in 1., that is, how to sample r such that P(r) = 2r. Let X be the random variable such that P(X = r) = 2r. Then, F_X(x) = \int_0^x 2r\,dr = x^2, and thus F_X^{-1}(y) = \sqrt{y}.

2.1 Code
With above in mind, we sample 10000 points on the unit disk, see Figure 1.

import numpy as np

R = np.vectorize(inv_cdf)(np.random.uniform(0, 1, N))
T = np.random.uniform(0, 2*np.pi, N)
points = [(r * np.cos(t), r * np.sin(t)) for r, t in zip(R, T)]

# 2. Make a scatter plot
x, y = zip(*points)
plt.scatter(x, y, s=1)

Listen first: slide the number of beads up to the last position, the continuous loop, and watch the stems settle onto the lines.

title: Why does a loop of string land exactly on the lines?
section: 1 · Newton’s law: the equation of motion
text:
1 · Newton’s law: the equation of motion
Mathematics used: derivatives, partial derivatives (explained), Taylor’s theorem (quoted) and integrals of sines and cosines.
Page 2 applied Newton’s law, mass times acceleration equals force, to each bead on a ring. Here we let the beads crowd together, keeping the loop’s size, its tension and its total mass fixed, and watch the bead equation turn into the equation of a continuous string.
1. Set up the loop. Measure position around the loop by the angle \theta, and choose units so that the loop has circumference 2\pi. Put N beads on it, bead j at \theta_j = jh, with spacing h = 2\pi/N. Let T be the string’s tension and \mu its mass per unit length, so each bead has mass m = \mu h. Write u(\theta, t) for the height of the loop at angle \theta and time t, so that bead j is at height u_j(t) = u(\theta_j, t).
2. Each bead is pulled toward its neighbors. The string pulls each bead along itself, on both sides. If the string makes a small angle \phi with the horizontal, the upward part of its pull is T\sin\phi; for a small angle \sin\phi \approx \tan\phi (both are about \phi in radians), and \tan\phi is the slope (page 2 draws it). So the pull from the right contributes the tension times the slope to the right, and the pull from the left minus the tension times the slope to the left: 
\begin{aligned} m\,\ddot u_j &= T\,\frac{u_{j+1} - u_j}{h} - T\,\frac{u_j - u_{j-1}}{h} \\ &= \frac{T}{h}\,\big(u_{j+1} - 2u_j + u_{j-1}\big). \end{aligned}
 Divide by the mass m = \mu h: 
\ddot u_j = \frac{T}{\mu}\cdot\frac{u_{j+1} - 2u_j + u_{j-1}}{h^2}.

3. The fraction measures how the string bends. The fraction compares each bead with its two neighbors. (u_{j+1} - u_j)/h is the slope just to the right of bead j, and (u_j - u_{j-1})/h the slope just to the left; their difference, divided by h once more, measures how fast the slope changes. Where the string bends down, the middle bead sits above the average of its neighbors, and the string pulls it down:

  
  
  
  
  θ − hθθ + h
  gap ≈ −h² u''/2

Taylor’s theorem makes this precise. It says that near \theta a smooth shape is its value, plus slope × h, plus half the second derivative × h^2, and so on; if you haven’t met it, the slope argument above is the whole idea. For a shape with four continuous derivatives, 
\begin{aligned} u(\theta \pm h) = u &\pm h\,u' + \tfrac{h^2}{2}u'' \\ &\pm \tfrac{h^3}{6}u''' + O(h^4), \end{aligned}
 where O(h^4) stands for terms no bigger than a constant times h^4. Add the two expansions and subtract 2u; the odd terms cancel in pairs: 
\begin{aligned} &u(\theta + h) - 2u(\theta) + u(\theta - h) \\ &\quad = h^2 u''(\theta) + O(h^4). \end{aligned}
 So the fraction equals u'' + O(h^2): the second derivative, the string’s curvature, up to an error that vanishes as the beads crowd together. The middle bead sits above the average of its neighbors by about -\tfrac{h^2}{2}u'', which is positive where the curve bends down (u'' < 0).
4. Let the beads crowd together. The height u now depends on two things, the angle and the time. Its derivative in time with the angle held fixed is written \partial u/\partial t, a partial derivative, and its derivative in angle with the time held fixed \partial u/\partial\theta; the second derivatives are also written u_{tt} and u_{\theta\theta}. As h \to 0, the bead equation becomes 
\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial t^2} = c^2\,\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial \theta^2}, \qquad c^2 = \frac{T}{\mu}.
 This is the wave equation. The constant c is the speed at which a bump travels around the loop; the second demo below shows it.
What we assumed. Small slopes, so that the tension stays T and its upward part is T times the slope; the same tension and mass per length everywhere; no stiffness, no air and no friction; and shapes smooth enough for Taylor’s theorem. As the beads multiplied, the circumference, T and \mu were held fixed, so each bead got lighter in proportion.

title: Why does a loop of string land exactly on the lines?
text:
2 · The operator
The right side of the wave equation is a fixed rule applied to the shape: take its second derivative in angle and multiply by c^2. That rule, with its sign reversed, is the loop’s operator. It acts on one shape f(\theta) at a time, so it is written with d rather than \partial. The minus sign makes Af positive at a bump, where f'' < 0, so the force -Af pulls the bump back down. The loop has no ends; what it imposes instead is that every shape closes up after one turn, and that condition is part of the operator. If you read page 2: there the operator was \frac{T}{mh}K = \frac{c^2}{h^2}K, and -K/h^2 is the second difference divided by h^2, which becomes the second derivative as the beads crowd together; so A is the continuous version of page 2’s matrix.

The loop’s operator. The equation of motion is 
\begin{gathered} u_{tt} = -A\,u, \\ A = -c^2\,\frac{d^2}{d\theta^2}, \qquad c^2 = \frac{T}{\mu}, \end{gathered}
 acting on shapes that close up after one turn, f(\theta + 2\pi) = f(\theta). In words: A takes a shape and returns minus its curvature, times c^2: the restoring force per unit mass, reversed.

title: Why does a loop of string land exactly on the lines?
text:
3 · Its spectrum
A mode is a shape that the operator only rescales: AX = \lambda X for some number \lambda. The shape X is an eigenfunction of A, and \lambda its eigenvalue. Released in that shape, the loop keeps it and swings at the angular frequency \omega = \sqrt\lambda, as on page 1. The list of all eigenvalues is the spectrum of A. Here is the whole computation.
1. Try a wave with n crests. A wave with n crests around the loop is \cos n\theta. Its second derivative is -n^2\cos n\theta, so 
\begin{gathered} A\cos n\theta = c^2n^2\cos n\theta, \\ A\sin n\theta = c^2n^2\sin n\theta . \end{gathered}
 A wave n times shorter is pulled back n^2 times harder. In plain words: squeeze a wave into half the length, at the same height, and it bends 4 times as sharply (the slope doubles, and it changes over half the distance: 2 × 2 = 4), so the pull is 4 times as strong.
2. Ask which waves close up, to find every eigenfunction. The equation AX = \lambda X says X'' = -(\lambda/c^2)\,X.

If \lambda = 0, then X = a + b\theta, which closes up after one turn only when b = 0. Eigenvalue 0 belongs to the constant shape: the whole loop lifted at once, which makes no sound.
If \lambda > 0, write \lambda = c^2s^2 with s > 0. Then X = a\cos s\theta + b\sin s\theta, a wave that repeats every 2\pi/s radians. It closes up after one full turn exactly when 2\pi is a whole number of these periods, that is, when s is a whole number n. Eigenvalue c^2n^2, eigenfunctions \cos n\theta and \sin n\theta.
A negative \lambda is impossible: the proof fold below shows that A has no negative eigenvalues.




Reader questionThe equation of one wave has one frequency in it. Where does an infinite list come from?

In the equation u'' + k^2u = 0, the number k is chosen in advance, and for each k it has the two solutions \cos k\theta and \sin k\theta. The eigenvalue question runs the other way: for which k does a solution go once around the loop and come back to itself? Every whole number k does, and nothing limits how many times a wave may wind around, so the list never ends. The count matches the number of ways the system can move: N beads have N eigenvalues, counted with repetitions, and a continuous loop has infinitely many.
For readers who know functional analysis: on an infinite straight string, with no loop to close up and no ends, every k \ge 0 gives a bounded wave e^{ikx} and the spectrum is the whole half-line [0, \infty). Strictly, these waves are not eigenfunctions, because \int|e^{ikx}|^2\,dx is infinite. This is one reason the general definition of spectrum is more than a list of eigenvalues. A bounded instrument, closed up or with ends that are not too irregular, has a discrete list.


3. Each eigenvalue gives a frequency. The motion \cos(n\theta)\cos(\omega t) solves u_{tt} = -Au when \omega^2 = \lambda_n = c^2n^2: differentiate it twice in t, apply A, and compare. Here \omega is the angular frequency, in radians per second, and the frequency in hertz is \omega/2\pi. So mode n sounds at 
f_n = \frac{\sqrt{\lambda_n}}{2\pi} = \frac{c\,n}{2\pi} = n\,f_1 .
 (In ordinary units, for a loop of circumference \ell, this is f_n = nc/\ell: the time for a bump to travel once around, \ell/c, is the period of the lowest mode.)
Why the frequency is proportional to n: every wave travels at the same speed. A shape that slides around the loop unchanged at speed c, u = g(\theta - ct), solves the wave equation for every shape g: both u_{tt} and c^2u_{\theta\theta} equal c^2g''. So on the loop a long wave and a short wave travel at the same speed c = \sqrt{T/\mu}, set by the tension and the mass per length alone. Each mode is two such waves running in opposite directions, 
\begin{aligned} \cos n\theta\,\cos nct &= \tfrac12\cos n(\theta - ct) \\ &\quad + \tfrac12\cos n(\theta + ct), \end{aligned}
 and a wave with n crests running at speed c brings n crests past a fixed point in the time one crest takes to go around. That is why mode n swings n times as fast as mode 1. Both facts are needed: the whole number of crests, and the common speed. On a ring of beads, short waves travel more slowly than long ones (stage 4), and on a stiff piano wire faster (page 7); in both cases the frequencies leave the whole numbers.



Reader questionHow is a mode’s shape related to its swinging in time?

Both come from separating variables. Look for a motion in which the shape stays fixed and only its size changes: u = X(\theta)\,q(t). Substituting into u_{tt} = c^2u_{\theta\theta} and dividing by Xq gives q''/q = c^2X''/X. The left side depends only on t and the right only on \theta. Changing t alone cannot change the right side, so the left side cannot change either; the same holds the other way round, so both sides equal one constant. That constant cannot be positive, because A has no negative eigenvalues (proof fold below), so we call it -\omega^2. That splits the equation in two. In time, q'' = -\omega^2 q, so q = \cos(\omega t + \phi), times any constant: the mass on a spring. (For \omega = 0 the solution is q = a + bt instead: the loop drifts as a whole.) In space, AX = -c^2X'' = \omega^2 X with X periodic: the eigenvalue problem for A, with \lambda = \omega^2, which allows only \omega = cn. The space part chooses the frequency, and the time part swings at it. The time factor is a cosine, for every nonzero frequency, for every instrument in this series, because every operator here has no negative eigenvalues and every equation has two time derivatives and no friction term; damping, added on page 7, multiplies the cosine by a decaying factor. Everything instrument-specific lives in the space part.



The loop’s spectrum. Eigenfunctions: the constant, and \cos n\theta and \sin n\theta for n = 1, 2, 3, \dots Eigenvalues: \lambda_n = c^2n^2, that is 0, c^2, 4c^2, 9c^2, \dots; each with n \ge 1 belongs to two eigenfunctions, the same wave shifted by a quarter of a wavelength. Frequencies: f_n = \sqrt{\lambda_n}/2\pi = n f_1 with f_1 = c/2\pi. In words: the eigenvalues are c^2 times perfect squares, so the frequencies, their square roots divided by 2\pi, are exactly whole-number multiples of one frequency.




ProofNo negative eigenvalues, and different waves are perpendicular uses integration by parts

No eigenvalue is negative. For periodic shapes f and g, integrate by parts twice. The boundary terms are values at \theta = 2\pi minus values at \theta = 0, which cancel because the shapes are periodic: 
\int_0^{2\pi} (Af)\,g\,d\theta = -c^2\!\int_0^{2\pi} f''g\,d\theta = c^2\!\int_0^{2\pi} f'g'\,d\theta = -c^2\!\int_0^{2\pi} f g''\,d\theta = \int_0^{2\pi} f\,(Ag)\,d\theta .
 An operator with this property is called symmetric, by analogy with a symmetric matrix. (With the right choice of allowed shapes it is also self-adjoint, the stronger property that the spectral theorem in the complex-numbers fold further down needs.) If Af = \lambda f with f not identically zero, take g = f in the middle expression: \lambda\int_0^{2\pi} f^2\,d\theta = c^2\int_0^{2\pi}(f')^2\,d\theta \ge 0, so \lambda \ge 0. (For a complex-valued f, use \int f\bar f\,d\theta = \int |f|^2\,d\theta instead, as in the complex-numbers fold further down; the same computation shows that \lambda is real and at least 0.)
Eigenfunctions for different eigenvalues are perpendicular, in the sense used below: \int_0^{2\pi} \cos n\theta\cos m\theta\,d\theta = 0 for n \ne m, and similarly for sines and for a sine against a cosine. This can be checked directly with the product formulas for cosines, and it also follows from the symmetry above, just as for a symmetric matrix.
For readers who know functional analysis: A is not defined on every square-integrable function, only on those with two derivatives in L^2, the Sobolev space H^2(S^1). On that domain it is self-adjoint, not merely symmetric: in Fourier coefficients it is multiplication by c^2n^2 on the sequences with \sum n^4|c_n|^2 < \infty. That there is no spectrum besides these eigenvalues follows from the completeness of the eigenfunctions, proved in the complex-numbers fold further down.


4. Every shape is a sum of these waves. Whether every shape of a string can be built from these simple waves was argued over for decades in the 18th century, from the 1740s on, by Jean d’Alembert, Leonhard Euler and Daniel Bernoulli. D’Alembert showed in 1747 that a string can move in essentially any smooth shape. Bernoulli held that every vibration is a sum of simple modes, which for a string are sine-shaped. Euler, who allowed a plucked string’s sharp corner as a starting shape, objected that a sum of sines could not represent such arbitrary shapes, and d’Alembert doubted that such a sum was physical at all.
Bernoulli was right, in a sense that took mathematicians more than a century to make precise. Every shape of the loop, corners included, is a sum of its eigenfunctions: its Fourier series, 
\begin{aligned} f(\theta) = \frac{a_0}{2} &+ \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\big(a_n\cos n\theta \\ &\qquad + b_n\sin n\theta\big). \end{aligned}
 The doubt is natural, since every wave is smooth and a corner is not, but an infinite sum of smooth waves need not be smooth.
How much of each wave a shape contains. The waves are perpendicular, in the sense of integrals: for whole numbers n \ne m, 
\begin{gathered} \int_0^{2\pi}\cos n\theta\,\cos m\theta\,d\theta = 0, \\ \int_0^{2\pi}\sin n\theta\,\sin m\theta\,d\theta = 0, \end{gathered}
 while \int_0^{2\pi}\cos n\theta\,\sin m\theta\,d\theta = 0 for all n and m, and \int_0^{2\pi}\cos^2 n\theta\,d\theta = \int_0^{2\pi}\sin^2 n\theta\,d\theta = \pi for n \ge 1. (To check them, turn each product into a sum with \cos A\cos B = \tfrac12[\cos(A - B) + \cos(A + B)] and its relatives for sines; every cosine or sine of a nonzero whole-number multiple of \theta integrates to zero over a full turn.) These integrals are the continuous version of the dot product: for two columns of bead heights, \sum_j u_j v_j\,h is a dot product times h, and as the beads crowd together it becomes \int f g\,d\theta. Multiply both sides of the series by \cos m\theta and integrate from 0 to 2\pi: every term drops out except the one with n = m, which leaves \pi a_m. So 
\begin{gathered} a_n = \frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} f(\theta)\cos n\theta\,d\theta, \\ b_n = \frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} f(\theta)\sin n\theta\,d\theta, \end{gathered}
 just as a vector’s component along an axis is its dot product with that axis. (The constant term is written a_0/2 so that the same formula also gives a_0: for n = 0, \int_0^{2\pi}\cos^2 0\,d\theta = 2\pi, not \pi.)



PreciselyThe same series with complex numbers, and why every shape is a sum of waves uses complex numbers; the second half, functional analysis

With complex numbers. With Euler’s formula e^{in\theta} = \cos n\theta + i\sin n\theta, the pair \cos n\theta, \sin n\theta can be traded for the pair e^{in\theta}, e^{-in\theta}, and A e^{in\theta} = c^2n^2 e^{in\theta}. The Fourier series becomes 
f(\theta) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} c_n\,e^{in\theta}, \qquad c_n = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} f(\theta)\,e^{-in\theta}\,d\theta ,
 with c_{\pm n} = (a_n \mp i b_n)/2 for n \ge 1 and c_0 = a_0/2. The perpendicularity above becomes \langle e^{in\theta}, e^{im\theta}\rangle = 0 for n \ne m, for the inner product \langle f, g\rangle = \int_0^{2\pi} f\,\bar g\,d\theta; the bar, complex conjugation, is what makes \langle f, f\rangle a positive number for complex-valued f. The natural space of shapes is L^2(S^1), all functions on the circle S^1 with \int_0^{2\pi}|f|^2\,d\theta finite: the shapes of finite “total squared height”.
Every shape is a sum of eigenfunctions. The functions e^{in\theta}/\sqrt{2\pi}, n \in \mathbb{Z}, form an orthonormal basis of L^2(S^1). That is, for every f in L^2(S^1), 
\Big\| f - \sum_{|n| \le M} c_n e^{in\theta} \Big\| \to 0 \quad (M \to \infty), \qquad \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|f|^2\,d\theta = \sum_n |c_n|^2 ,
 the second identity being Parseval’s.
Why it needs a proof. For a symmetric N\times N matrix, N perpendicular eigenvectors automatically span everything, because the space has dimension N. Here there are infinitely many eigenfunctions and the space is infinite-dimensional, so one has to show that no shape is perpendicular to all of them. One standard proof shows that trigonometric sums can approximate any continuous periodic function uniformly (Fejér’s theorem), and that continuous functions are dense in L^2. See Stein and Shakarchi, chapters 2 and 3.
Pointwise. Convergence in L^2 is convergence of the total squared error. At individual points more care is needed: there are continuous functions whose Fourier series diverge at a point. For the shapes on this page, continuous and made of straight pieces, the series converges at every point. The plucked triangle’s coefficients shrink like 1/n^2, which is why a few terms already look right in the demo.
What it took. The old argument could not be settled until “sum” had a precise meaning for infinitely many terms. Fourier claimed such expansions for arbitrary functions in his 1807 work on heat. Dirichlet proved in 1829 that the series converges at every point for a broad class of functions, including shapes with corners; the L^2 statement above belongs to the early 20th century; and that the Fourier series of every L^2 function converges at almost every point was proved only in 1966, by Lennart Carleson (Wikipedia). In the L^2 sense, Bernoulli was right, and a corner is no obstacle.
The pattern for every later page. Each instrument’s operator A will be self-adjoint and nonnegative, and (A + 1)^{-1} will be a compact operator. The spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators then gives the same three facts as here: a list of real eigenvalues growing to infinity, perpendicular eigenfunctions, and an expansion of every shape in them. Only the list and the shapes change.

The demo at the top is this page’s spectrum diagram; the table below gives some of its numbers. On the continuous loop, mode n sits exactly on the line n×, at f_n = n f_1 from the result box. With a few beads, the stems sit below the lines, the higher modes furthest below; on a ring of N beads, mode k’s frequency divided by mode 1’s is \sin(\pi k/N)/\sin(\pi/N) (page 2), which tends to k as N grows. Why beads fall short. A bead feels only its two neighbors. When a crest is many beads wide, that is enough to sense the bend almost exactly. When a crest is only a few beads wide, the neighbors sit partway down the wave, and the bead underestimates how sharply the string bends: the second difference is smaller than h^2 times the curvature. So the pull is weaker than n² times, and the frequency falls short of n×, the more so the shorter the wave. In terms of speed: on the beads a short wave travels more slowly than a long one. Crowd in more beads and any given wave becomes many beads wide: its shortfall vanishes, and every wave travels at c.

title: Why does a loop of string land exactly on the lines?
text:
5 · What we hear
Why exactly on the lines. Mode n swings at f_n = n f_1, so every mode returns to its starting position after the time 1/f_1 = 2\pi/c; the whole motion repeats, and the sound it makes is a note at f_1, when f_1 is in the range we hear as pitch. The tension, the mass and the size of the loop cannot spoil this; they only set f_1 = c/2\pi. The whole-number lines of the pitch ruler come from two facts: a wave on a loop must close up, so it has a whole number of crests, and every wave travels at the same speed c, so a wave with n crests swings n times as fast as the lowest. Press the first demo’s button at a few bead counts: with few beads the mix sounds less clear; on the loop the modes fuse into one note (page 0).
Released, each wave swings at its own frequency. From rest in the shape f, with the coefficients a_n, b_n of its Fourier series, 
\begin{aligned} u(\theta, t) &= \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} q_n(\theta)\,\cos(2\pi f_n t), \\ q_n(\theta) &= a_n\cos n\theta + b_n\sin n\theta. \end{aligned}
 The sound is this sum: each mode contributes a pure tone at its own frequency f_n, as strong as the shape contains it. The demos synthesize exactly that: the button in the first demo adds the first modes’ frequencies, mode 1 set to 196 Hz, quieter for higher modes; the “Hear the loop” button in the demo below adds the plucked shape’s modes with the strengths from its Fourier series.

title: Why does a loop of string land exactly on the lines?
text:
What we found
The loop’s operator, A = -c^2\,d^2/d\theta^2 on shapes that close up, has the spectrum \lambda_n = c^2n^2, so its frequencies are exactly 0, 1, 2, 3, … times one base frequency: each wave has a whole number n of crests, and every wave travels at the same speed c. Every shape is a sum of these waves, its Fourier series, so a plucked loop repeats exactly and sounds a note. The next page ties a string down at both ends.
